items.title: Rahal Mekkaoui remplace Madiha Khayr à la tête du groupe parlementaire de l'Istiqlal
items.description: Tel que prévu, le groupe Istiqlalien de l'unité et de l'égalitarisme à la Chambre des représentants a élu, ce lundi matin, Rahal Mekkaoui à la présidence du groupe parlementaire, succédant ainsi à Madiha Khayr, démise dimanche de ses fonctions au sein du gouvernement. Cette élection s'est déroulée lors d'une réunion tenue en présence de Nizar Baraka, secrétaire général du Parti de l'Istiqlal, afin d'officialiser la désignation du nouveau chef de file de la formation de la balance au sein de la première chambre. Rahal Mekkaoui figurait en position de favori pour assumer cette responsabilité, fort du soutien affirmé du comité exécutif du parti. Pour rappel, Madiha Khayr avait été nommée vendredi dernier au poste de ministre déléguée chargée de la Formation professionnelle et de la Qualification auprès du ministre de l’Éducation nationale, du Préscolaire, de la Formation professionnelle et de la Qualification, ce qui avait entraîné la vacance automatique de son siège de présidente du groupe en application des dispositions légales sur le cumul des mandats. Toutefois, en raison de la controverse suscitée par la diffusion de documents judiciaires et médicaux attribués à la ministre déléguée, le Roi Mohammed VI a accédé, dimanche, à la demande de la Cheffe du gouvernement visant à démettre Madiha Khayr de ses fonctions ministérielles, conformément au quatrième paragraphe de l'article 47 de la Constitution. The post Rahal Mekkaoui remplace Madiha Khayr à la tête du groupe parlementaire de l'Istiqlal appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Mamou : le Championnat national de Sambo et la Coupe nationale 2026 mobilisent les athlètes guinéens
items.description: La ville de Mamou a accueilli, du 14 au 18 octobre 2026, le Championnat national de Sambo couplé à la Coupe nationale. Organisée dans l'enceinte de la Maison des jeunes, cette compétition a réuni des athlètes venus de plusieurs localités du pays autour de cette discipline de combat qui attire de plus en plus de jeunes Guinéens. Le Sambo est un sport de combat qui combine différentes techniques de lutte et de combat, notamment celles du judo, de la boxe et du kick-boxing. À travers cette compétition nationale, les responsables de la discipline entendent renforcer sa promotion et favoriser son développement sur l'ensemble du territoire guinéen. Selon Mamadou Sadigou Bah, président de la Fédération guinéenne de Sambo et disciplines associées, le choix de Mamou s'inscrit dans une volonté d'élargir la pratique de cette discipline « Dans notre vision de promotion, de vulgarisation et d'extension du Sambo, nous avons choisi d'organiser ces compétitions à Mamou », a-t-il expliqué. Les athlètes participants provenaient notamment de Kouroussa, Kankan, Kérouané, Mandiana, Siguiri, Mamou, Dalaba, Pita, Fria et Kamsar, ainsi que de trois clubs de Conakry. Au terme des confrontations, plusieurs combattants se sont distingués dans les différentes catégories du Sambo combat et du Sambo sportif. Les résultats par catégorie 1. Catégorie des 79 kg – Sambo combat garçons Médaille d'or : Abdoul Karim Touré (ISGF). Médaille d'argent : Ayouba Camara (Club Dragon). Médailles de bronze : Mohamed Magassouba (Lion Club) et Aboubacar Demba Tounkara (Kouroussa). 2. Catégorie des 79 kg – Sambo sportif Médaille d'or : Djibril Keïta (Club Dalil). Médaille d'argent : Aboubacar Camara (Club Dalil). 3. Catégorie des 71 kg – Sambo sportif Médaille d'or : Aboubacar Camara (Club Dalil). Médaille d'argent : Abdoul Karim Diallo (Club Dalil). Médaille de bronze : Mamadou Diallo (Club Dalil). 4. Catégorie des 71 kg – Sambo combat Médaille d'or : Mamadi Kantè (Lion Club). Médaille d'argent : Laye Fodé Konaté (Lion Club). Médailles de bronze : Oumar Keïta et Issiaga Condè (Dragon Noir). 5. Catégorie des 64 kg – Sambo combat garçons Médaille d'or : Adama Condè (Waza Club Kolenda). Médaille d'argent : Mohamed Lamine Sylla (ISGF). Médailles de bronze : Daouda Keïta (ISGF) et Kerfalla Cissé (Lion Junior). 6. Catégorie des 58 kg – Sambo combat Médaille d'or : Mohamed Yansané (Mamou). Médaille d'argent : Saifoulaye Barry (Club Dalil). Médailles de bronze : Mamadi Condè et Jean Claude Telliano (Yin-Yong Club). 7. Catégorie des 58 kg – Sambo sportif Médaille d'or : Aboubacar Seck. Médaille d'argent : Moussa Oularé. Médaille de bronze : Alpha Saliou Sow. 8. Catégorie des 53 kg – Sambo sportif Médaille d'or : Boubacar Biro Watson (Club Dalil). Médaille d'argent : Touré Mohamed Lamine (ISGF). Médailles de bronze : Abdoulaye Bakayoko et Mamady Kaba (Club Dalil). 9. Catégorie des 50 kg – Sambo sportif filles Médaille d'or : Aïssatou Keïta (Club Dalil). Médaille d'argent : Aminata Camara (Club Dalil). Médailles de bronze : Aïssatou Soumah (Club Dalil) et Bintou Sylla Diallo (Mamou). 10. Catégorie des 50 kg – Sambo sportif garçons Médaille d'or : Mohamed Touré (Club Dalil). Médaille d'argent : Ibrahim Touré (Club Dalil). Médailles de bronze : Abdoul Karim Bah et Boubacar Soumah (Club Dalil). 11. Catégorie des enfants 27 kg – Sambo sportif Médaille d'or : Aboubacar Sidiki Diallo (Club Dalil). Médaille d'argent : Thierno Hamidou Baldé (Mamou). Médailles de bronze : Ansoumane Camara (Club Dalil) et Ibrahima Sory Diané (ISGF). Cette compétition constitue ainsi une occasion pour les athlètes de mesurer leur niveau, de valoriser leurs performances, de contribuer à la visibilité du Sambo en Guinée et de préparer les compétitions africaines et mondiales.

items.title: Uefa gives Infantino two-week deadline to release key documents
items.description: European governing body Uefa has told Fifa it must release key documents and answer all questions relating to its governance and decision-making by a deadline of 2 November. At the Fifa Council on Thursday, president Gianni Infantino apologised for his World Cup sell-off plan – but failed to offer a full explanation for how the proposal was devised. In the letter seen by BBC Sport, Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis said that world football’s governing body had failed to address “a number of fundamental questions”. “Others remain unanswered, and the information and documentation requested have not been provided,” it read. The letter included eight pages containing 42 questionscovering a number of issues, from the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) private investment, to the Fifa Peace Prize and the controversial suspended ban given to USA striker Folarin Balogun at the World Cup. “The withdrawal of FFE, the acknowledgement of mistakes and the announcement of ‘potential governance reforms’ do not answer how the relevant decisions were taken or why the Fifa Council was not involved at the appropriate stage,” it continued. “Any refusal to disclose information or documents should be justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon. “These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the Fifa Council – nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them.” Uefa did not outline what steps it intended to take should Fifa not meet the deadline, but will hope it adds to the pressure on Infantino ahead of November 18, the cut-off date for any candidates to confirm they are standing against him in next year’s presidential election. The questions were first put to Infantino at the Fifa Council last week, with Infantino then asking that they were submitted in writing. Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt – a Fifa vice-president – said afterwards that “if he doesn’t answer those questions, he’s not fit to be Fifa president”. Fifa has been approached for comment. Fifa faces question on FFE and funding to associations Uefa has posed a great number of questions about FFE. “When was the idea of FFE first explored, by whom and with what objective?” Uefa asked. “Who within Fifa authorised the development of the project, and which members of the Fifa administration were involved? “What concrete measures will Fifa put in place to ensure that the shortcomings identified in the FFE process cannot occur again in the future?” Uefa goes on to ask about the circumstances surrounding Infantino’s initial presentation of the FFE plan to senior Fifa executives. In particular, it raises a question about a potential investigation into Fifa in the United States. BBC Sport has approached Uefa to ascertain what this is in relation to. “According to information received from several sources, two days before the vote by the bureau of the management board on the FFE proposal, the Fifa president informed members of the management board that the US authorities were investigating Fifa’s administration,” Uefa claim. “Can he confirm whether such a statement was made and, if so, explain the information on which it was based, the reasons for raising it at that particular moment and whether he considered the potential pressure it might place on members immediately before their decision on FFE?” Uefa requested information on whether Infantino would have held or expected to hold any position, role or function in FFE, either during or following his tenure as Fifa president. The relationship with Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital was covered in detail, asking why an agreement granting exclusivity to the company was signed without prior consultation of the Fifa Council. “Why was Thrive Capital selected as lead investor, without any competitive tendering process and under conditions of strict confidentiality, despite its links to the family of the recipient of the Fifa Peace Prize?” Uefa asked. Kushner is the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law, while the US president was awarded the Peace Prize. Uefa also requested answer about the award of the Peace Prize, specifically who decided to establish it, for what purpose, and who decided that Trump should receive it. When the FFE plan was revealed in the days following the World Cup final, Infantino told the 211 member associations (MAs) they would receive $40m (£30m) if they backed it. He then set a deadline of 19 September for federations to accept his plans if they wanted to access an initial $20m (£15m). However, once the scheme was abandoned, Uefa and Concacaf called on Fifa to pay at least $10m (£7.5m) from its cash reserves to each of the MAs and, last week, Infantino agreed, proposing to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn). The releasing of cash from its reserves will result in double the level of planned distribution funding for MAs from 2027 to 2030, with $25m (£19m) available per member association. “Why was substantially increased funding for MAs presented in connection with FFE and external investment, rather than being financed directly from Fifa’s own resources?” Uefa has asked. “Given Fifa’s strong financial position, why was it considered necessary to seek investment from private investors? What financial or strategic advantages would such an arrangement have offered compared with funding football development directly from Fifa’s own resources, particularly in light of Fifa’s subsequent proposal to do precisely that on a substantially increased scale?” While Fifa is yet to respond, sources have indicated its ability to answer certain questions are restricted by the legal action that Uefa has launched. Last month, it filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland. Infantino has faced intense scrutiny over the case of Balogun, who avoided an immediate suspension after being sent off at the World Cup. Balogun’s ban was lifted by Fifa’s disciplinary committee, after US President Donald Trump asked Infantino for the decision to be reviewed. Fifa insisted the committee was independent but its legal committee is now reviewing a proposal to amend its disciplinary code, which would prevent a repeat, with an update due in December. Uefa has asked why this is necessary. “President Trump publicly acknowledged having called the Fifa president to request a review of the Balogun disciplinary case. What exactly did he ask him to do, and what was his response?”, Uefa has asked. “Would the case have been reviewed in the absence of his intervention?” “Following that conversation, did the Fifa president or the Fifa secretary general communicate with anyone within Fifa, including members of the administration or the chair of the disciplinary committee, concerning the Balogun case? If so, could Fifa specify with whom, when and the nature of those communications? “We also request all correspondence and other communications concerning the case between the chair of the disciplinary committee and the Fifa administration, including the Fifa president and Fifa’s chief legal officer. “Could Fifa provide the full written reasons for the decision in the Balogun case, including the information and evidence before the disciplinary committee? “Who decided that the matter should be determined by a single member of the committee, on what basis…and what were the exceptional circumstances relied upon to justify the decision?” Uefa also asked why no disciplinary action was taken against DR Congo after the African nation reportedly played an ineligible player in World Cup qualifying. Usually, this would result in the country being disqualified but no action was taken. Infantino quizzed over ‘additional salary’ claim Reports in the lead-up last week’s Fifa Council suggested Infantino had received an additional salary from Fifa’s US World Cup organising entity (FWC2026 US Inc.) which was not disclosed in Fifa’s annual report. Uefa has asked Fifa to “clarify the nature, amount and basis of these payments, why they were not disclosed and whether they were reviewed and approved by the competent Fifa bodies.” It added: “Could Fifa also confirm whether the additional remuneration was treated as taxable income and whether the corresponding income tax was paid?” Fifa has previously denied paying Infantino a second salary, and insisted it complies with all reporting requirements in relation to compensation, saying it “strongly rejects any claims that it has failed to disclose any financial information and has violated Fifa’s statutes.” Uefa also asked about reported “advanced discussions involving the US president and individuals associated with him concerning a Fifa cryptocurrency”, and the $75m (£56.3m) investment in Palestine via Trump’s Board of Peace. The extended 27-minute half-time interval during the World Cup final and introduction of mandatory hydration breaks were also raised. Uefa wanted answers on the “seven-year, $4m (£3m) lease of office premises in Trump Tower, New York, involving Eric Trump, for premises reportedly unused for much of the year”. It wrote: “These matters, taken together, raise questions that extend beyond the ordinary institutional relationship between Fifa and the government of a World Cup host country. “Could Fifa provide a detailed explanation of these arrangements and interventions, including the decision-making processes followed, the identification and management of any potential conflicts of interest, the financial implications for Fifa and the extent to which the competent Fifa bodies were informed or consulted?” Also brought up was the impartiality of the chair of the Fifa electoral committee before next year’s presidential election who, Uefa says, “attended the entire 2026 World Cup as an accredited individual, with his expenses covered by Fifa for more than five weeks”. It also asked for a full list of the guests seated in the VIP and VVIP sections “including their names, positions and the reasons for their invitations”.

items.title: Dahra : un point Wave braqué, 8 millions de FCFA emportés
items.description: Un point de transfert d’argent Wave, situé sur la route nationale à Dahra, près de la radio Ferlo FM, a été la cible d’un braquage à main armée lundi soir, aux environs de 20 heures. Les assaillants sont repartis avec une somme estimée à 8 millions de FCFA. Selon des témoignages recueillis sur place, plusieurs individus armés ont fait irruption dans le kiosque avant d’ouvrir le feu avec des armes à balles réelles pour semer la panique et contraindre les occupants à leur remettre la caisse. Avant de prendre la fuite, les malfaiteurs ont également caillassé le véhicule du gérant. Ils ont ensuite disparu dans la nuit. Alertée, la brigade de gendarmerie de Dahra s’est rendue sur les lieux pour effectuer les constatations d’usage et ouvrir une enquête en vue d’identifier les auteurs de cette attaque. Abdoulaye SADIO (Correspondant)

items.title: Americans Are Spending More Money to Drive Worse Cars
items.description: For the first time since the dawn of the automobile, the majority of new cars are not powered exclusively by gasoline: So far in 2026, electric vehicles and hybrids are outselling traditional gas-powered cars. As oil prices have gone up and up since the start of the war in Iran, drivers from Hanoi to Hamburg are picking up EVs like never before. According to the energy think tank Ember, 49 countries have broken EV-sales records this year. The prime minister of Thailand recently ditched his Rolls-Royce and commuted to work in an all-electric BYD Sealion. And then there’s the United States. For all the angst over high gas prices, EVs accounted for just 6.4 percent of new-car sales in the U.S. from July to September. That’s a slight rise from January, before the beginning of the war with Iran—but just barely. The U.S. has long been something of an EV laggard, full of drivers ( and a president ) who are skeptical of battery-powered cars. But even as gas prices have jumped from $3 to $4.50 over the past year, drivers won’t budge. America’s car fleet was never going to flip overnight. No one forks over $50,000 for a Tesla the moment gas hits $5 a gallon. “If gas prices are higher for a little while,” Elaine Buckberg, a senior fellow at Harvard University’s Salata Institute for Climate and Sustainability and a former executive at General Motors, told me. “People say, ‘Oh, this is going to pass. I’m not going to go and change what vehicle I own.’” But when high gas prices linger for half a year or longer, Buckberg added, the direction of the car industry can shift. The shortages and lines of the 1970s helped kill the mid-century land yacht . In the 2000s, record-high gas prices tempered the craze for gas-guzzling SUVs and pushed millions of Americans to buy hybrids like the Toyota Prius. Now drivers have a real alternative to the whims of the world oil market. They’re just not taking it. Americans are not all gasoline loyalists who’ve forsworn battery power. In fact, most drivers now say that they are strongly considering an EV as their next vehicle, and the trend is even stronger among people under 35. Pre-owned EVs are surging, but they represent a sliver of the used-car market, because so few of them are out there. The biggest winner from the gasoline spike has been the plain old hybrid, the green-car solution of the George W. Bush years. Sales in the U.S. have jumped 27 percent over the past year. To some degree, Americans aren’t making the leap for several long-standing reasons: EVs are too expensive, and the options are lacking. Because the U.S. effectively bans electric cars made in China, we are cut off from buying something such as the BYD Dolphin Surf, an electric sedan that sells for about $22,000 in Europe. Many of the models that drivers are familiar with still cannot be had as an EV. Toyotas such as the RAV4 and Camry now come only as hybrids; last year, Ford killed the electric version of the F-150 pickup truck, this country’s most popular vehicle, citing low sales. Ford is now hyping up a roughly $30,000 electric pickup truck, but that won’t arrive until 2027. Meanwhile, America’s only electric minivan is the struggling Volkswagen ID. Buzz, a modern take on the flower-power bus. And although Tesla’s cars have a lot going for them, plenty of Americans say they won’t touch the brand because of Elon Musk. In short, the EV market is full of holes. [ Read: The great Tesla sell-off ] That said, it’s hard not to look at tepid EV sales and wonder whether Americans have lost the plot on electric cars. The price gap between gas and electric cars is closing; more EVs are now available for under $40,000. Charging networks are expanding, and battery ranges are climbing. Compared with even just a year or two ago, buying an electric car comes with fewer trade-offs. And in plenty of ways, EVs are just better. They’re zippy and fun to drive. They don’t require much of the routine maintenance, such as oil changes, that make car ownership annoying. They can do all sorts of things that fossil-fuel burners cannot: refuel at home, keep a house’s lights on during a blackout, store luggage in a “frunk.” But if gas that’s creeping up on $5 a gallon isn’t enough to persuade people to go electric, what will? When I posed the question to Buckberg, she told me about research she’d worked on while at GM: Drivers were “happy to buy an EV—as long as they don’t have to give up anything they like about their current vehicle,” she said. In other words, it’s not enough for EVs to be good at what they’re good at—especially when relatively few Americans know someone who has one. They need to match the things that gas cars are good at too. Fast chargers are spreading, but not fast enough to free us from the mental load of worrying about where to refuel—something that’s been a given in a nation with a gas station at every corner. And what EVs can’t do yet ( unless you’re in China ) is recharge in as little time as it takes to pump gas. That’s something American drivers see as a prerequisite, even though most of us don’t regularly take very long road trips and drive an average of 30-some miles a day—a total easily handled by charging at home. There’s every reason to think that EVs will continue a gradual climb, Corey Cantor, the research director at the Zero Emission Transportation Association, told me. A new wave of hyper-capable electric cars is arriving in America, with ranges above 400 miles per charge. But if EVs really have to do everything gas-powered cars do—and more—before drivers give them a chance, it’ll be a long time before America embraces them en masse. We’re nowhere near the charging speeds that China has achieved nor the density of plugs that would rival the ubiquity of gas stations. Until then, Americans will keep pumping gas into worse cars while the rest of the world has long moved on.

items.description: Au Tchad, la saison des pluies s'achève, mais il n'a pas assez plu. Même dans le sud du pays, où les pluies sont habituellement plus abondantes, les précipitations ont été particulièrement faibles. items.title: Exiled critic of Rwandan president found beheaded
items.description: A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda. Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution. Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera’s head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend. The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad. His widow, Jeanne d’Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family’s safety. “It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don’t have security,” she said. According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death. Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration. Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice. In a statement on X, the RNC said: “Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?” His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile. In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa. Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government. Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics. “Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time,” he said. In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.

items.title: GH¢400m to be allocated for reclamation of galamsey destroyed lands, EPA and Blue Water Guards in 2027 Budget – Mahama
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has announced a plan to allocate GH¢400 million in the 2027 Budget for land reclamation and environmental protection activities. He said half of the allocation, GH¢200 million, will be used to reclaim 5,000 acres of land degraded by illegal mining [galamsey], while the remaining GH¢200 million will support the activities of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the Blue Water Guards. Speaking at the opening of the Mining in Motion 2026 Summit in Accra on Monday, October 19, 2026, President Mahama said the reclamation exercise would begin in 2027. “The planned reclamation exercise comes amid ongoing efforts by the government and mining companies to restore lands degraded by illegal mining. The damage caused by the activity nationwide is estimated at 12,000 acres,” President Mahama said. On October 14, 2026, the government and the Asantehene launched the Jimi Land Reclamation and River Watercourse Rehabilitation Project to restore 153 hectares of degraded land upstream of the Jimi Dam in the Ashanti Region. At Monday’s summit, President Mahama also cited efforts by mining companies and state institutions to reclaim degraded lands. He said Newmont had reclaimed nearly 800 acres of mined-out land and planted useful crops on the restored areas. He also said the Ghana Gold Board had awarded the Ghana Armed Forces a contract to reclaim 253 acres in the Tano Nimiri Forest Reserve, where work was ongoing. On measures to curb illegal mining in forest reserves, the President said illegal miners had encroached on 48 of the country’s 288 forest reserves. He explained that nine of the affected reserves had previously been designated as red zones because armed miners prevented forest guards from entering them. According to him, all nine reserves had since been cleared of illegal miners and were being prepared for reclamation. President Mahama also reported that authorities had confiscated more than 8,200 items associated with illegal mining, including 135 excavators, and recovered nearly 200 firearms. He said 6,060 excavators had been registered and detained at the ports, while 2,059 had been fitted with tracking devices to help authorities monitor their movements and use. The President added that 11 cooperatives had been trained in improved mining methods and were operational. He said the Ghana Gold Board was also financing small-scale artisanal mining using technology intended to reduce environmental destruction. President Mahama also announced a reforestation initiative being undertaken by the Ministry of Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation in partnership with the REDD+ programme. The initiative is expected to cover several parts of the country, including the Savannah regions.

items.title: Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders
items.description: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children. Mackenzie ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could “meet Jesus”. His doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was “evil”. Twenty-eight other leaders of his cult were also convicted of murder. They had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die. Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing. Delivering her eight-hour judgement in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie’s followers believed he was “Jesus’s mouthpiece”. One of his co-accused said Mackenzie had told his followers that anyone who “resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows”. Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called “weddings”. Those who died “were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus”, the judge said. One witness stated that a pregnant woman had been barred from nursing her newborn baby, who died 12 days later. “She was instructed to fast to death and follow her children,” the witness said. Mackenzie’s former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution. Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children. But this is the first time the pastor has faced a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November. He was arrested in 2023, after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie had led his followers from across the country. Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie. “I’m a happy man, that all persons have been convicted,” he told the BBC outside court. “All six of my children died in Shakahola forest,” Mwiti said ahead of the verdict, visibly emotional, holding a photograph of his family. “I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel.” More than 400 bodies were dug up in Shakahola forest Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day. “Every grave we found had at least three bodies,” James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. “Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old.” “We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive; the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another.” Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their “hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets”. Although many of Mackenzie’s followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are from people who were familiar to the community, as members of the cult often went to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana, which flows through the town. “We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest,” said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. “But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside.” Stephen Mwiti said he was happy with the verdict Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers to its branches across Kenya. His church ran a television station called Times TV, which broadcast his sermons from Malindi. His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as “evil”, healthcare as “against the doctrine” and digital identity cards as “the mark of the devil”. Mackenzie’s son, Dan Paul Mackenzie, said he worked as a cameraperson in the church. “The children would sit at the back, adults in the middle, and everyone would sing worship songs all morning.” The self-proclaimed pastor would start his fiery sermons at noon, some of which included “casting out demons”. This is the building from where Mackenzie broadcast his sermons The main church shut down in 2019, and Paul Mackenzie moved to Sthe hakahola forest, encouraging his followers to follow him. Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie’s church when he was eight years old and described him as his “spiritual father”, adding that he would “never say a bad word about him”. When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill, and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned. “My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believed that only God could heal me,” Shukrani said. The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. “We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal,” Shukrani said. By March 2023, when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. “We would carry someone out of the forest, but they were so frail that they would die in our arms,” explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers. Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest. He was ill and bedridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover. “My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie’s doctrine that medicine was evil,” Shukrani said. “I would have died if I wasn’t rescued from Shakahola forest.” Peter Shukrani says he would have died if he had stayed in the forest but still believes Mackenzie is a good man Many of the bodies are still unidentified owing to their advanced state of decomposition. In the court documents, several are referred to as “unknown male child” and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery. Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie’s followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was “a good person who cares for me”. “Mackenzie didn’t force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs,” Shukrani said before the verdict was announced. “I still love him and he is still my pastor.” In contrast Dan Mackenzie believed his father should be found guilty of murder. “He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing,” also speaking before the verdict.

items.title: Kenyan pastor, who told followers to starve for Jesus, convicted of 191 murders
items.description: A Kenyan court has convicted pastor Paul Mackenzie of murdering 191 people, including 190 children, after he allegedly directed members of his religious group to starve themselves and their children to death to “meet Jesus”. The BBC reported on Monday that 28 other leaders of the religious group were also convicted of murder. All the defendants had pleaded not guilty, repeatedly maintaining that nobody had been forced to die. Delivering an eight-hour judgement in the coastal city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie’s followers regarded him as “Jesus’s mouthpiece”. According to the report, one of Mackenzie’s co-accused told the court that the pastor had instructed followers to use violence against anyone who refused to fast. The co-accused said anyone who “resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows”. The judge also revealed that burials in the forest where the group operated were referred to as “weddings”, with those who died described as people who “were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus”. The court heard that 17 men from a nearby town were hired to excavate shallow graves in the forest, with some reportedly receiving as little as $8 (£6) a day. One of the gravediggers, identified as James, recounted the disturbing discoveries made during the exercise. “Every grave we found had at least three bodies,” James told the BBC. “Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old.” He added, “We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another.” The workers also reported finding children whose “hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets”. Another gravedigger, Salim Karisa, said some of the victims were known to residents of neighbouring Shakahola town, as members of the group regularly visited to purchase supplies and collect water from the River Galana. “We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest. But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside,” Karisa said. Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003, building a following of thousands over the next 16 years through church branches across Kenya. The church also ran a television station, Times TV, which aired his sermons from Malindi. His teachings reportedly described education as “evil”, healthcare as “against the doctrine” and digital identity cards as “the mark of the devil”. Mackenzie’s son, Dan Paul Mackenzie, said he worked as a cameraperson for the church and recalled how worship services were organised. “The children would sit at the back, adults in the middle, and everyone would sing worship songs all morning,” he said. The pastor usually began preaching at noon, with some sessions featuring what was described as “casting out demons”. After the church’s main branch shut down in 2019, Mackenzie relocated to Shakahola forest and encouraged his followers to move there. Among those who followed him was Peter Shukrani, 23, who relocated to the forest with his mother. He had joined the church at the age of eight and considered Mackenzie his “spiritual father”. Despite his experiences, Shukrani said he would “never say a bad word about him”. However, he fell ill while living in the forest, where medication was prohibited. His condition worsened after his mother discarded the medicines he needed. “My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me,” Shukrani said. He described the group’s living conditions, saying members stayed in mud houses scattered across the expansive forest. “We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal,” he said. The first bodies were discovered by local herders in March 2023, by which time hundreds of people had reportedly died. Karisa said some victims were so severely weakened by starvation that they died while being transported out of the forest. “We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms,” he said. Shukrani was among those rescued. He said he had been bedridden for weeks before his rescue and believed he would not have survived without intervention. “My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie’s doctrine that medicine was evil. I would have died if I wasn’t rescued from Shakahola forest,” he said. Many of the recovered bodies remain unidentified because of decomposition. Court records reportedly identify several victims as “unknown male child”, using the locations of their graves and the dates of discovery to distinguish them. Despite accounts of starvation, strangulation and bludgeoning among the victims, Shukrani continued to defend Mackenzie before the verdict. He described the pastor as “a good person who cares for me”. “Mackenzie didn’t force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs. I still love him and he is still my pastor,” Shukrani said. Dan Mackenzie, however, argued before the ruling that his father should be held responsible for the deaths because of his leadership position within the group. “He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing,” he said. The post Kenyan pastor, who told followers to starve for Jesus, convicted of 191 murders appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Sénatoriales en Guinée : la caution à 30 millions fg par candidat, les dépenses de campagne à 300 millions (DGE)
items.description: La Direction générale des élections (DGE) a fixé à 30 millions de francs guinéens la caution à verser par chaque candidat aux élections sénatoriales prévues le 20 décembre 2026. Le plafond des dépenses de campagne est, quant à lui, fixé à 300 millions de GNF par candidature. À l’approche des élections sénatoriales du 20 décembre 2026, le ministère de l’Administration du territoire et de la Décentralisation, à travers la Direction générale des élections (DGE), a précisé les modalités financières applicables aux candidats. Dans une décision référencée N° D/1166/MATD/DGE/2026, signée le 18 octobre 2026 par le directeur général adjoint de la DGE, Georges Abraham Sorry, l’autorité électorale fixe le montant de la caution, encadre les dépenses de campagne et précise les obligations financières des candidats. Une caution de 30 millions de francs guinéens L’article premier de la décision, pris en application de l’article 275 du Code électoral, fixe à 30 millions de francs guinéens le montant de la caution exigée de chaque candidat aux élections sénatoriales du 20 décembre 2026. S’agissant des modalités de versement, l’article 2 prévoit que la caution doit être déposée au Trésor public, contre récépissé, au plus tard cinquante jours avant la date du scrutin. Les fonds doivent être versés sur les comptes du Trésor public ouverts à la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée (BCRG). Selon la décision, un compte spécifique est prévu pour Conakry et pour chaque préfecture. Les dépenses de campagne plafonnées à 300 millions de GNF La DGE fixe également une limite aux dépenses électorales afin d’encadrer le financement des campagnes. Aux termes de l’article 3, le montant global des dépenses de campagne est plafonné à 300 millions de francs guinéens par candidature. L’article 4 interdit formellement aux candidats de dépasser ce plafond. Toute dépense excédentaire constitue, selon la décision, une violation des dispositions du Code électoral et expose son auteur aux sanctions prévues par la loi. La décision met également l’accent sur la traçabilité des ressources financières mobilisées pendant la campagne électorale. En application des articles 280 et 281 du Code électoral, chaque candidat est tenu de constituer un fonds électoral exclusivement destiné au financement de sa campagne. L’article 5 précise que chaque candidat doit ouvrir un compte de campagne auprès d’un établissement bancaire agréé. Ce compte doit permettre de retracer l’origine des fonds reçus ainsi que leur utilisation. La personne chargée des dépenses électorales ne peut effectuer de paiement ni engager de dépense en dehors de ce fonds électoral, précise la décision. Enfin, l’article 6 confie l’application de cette décision aux directions techniques, aux services d’appui, au conseiller juridique ainsi qu’aux démembrements de la Direction générale des élections. À travers ces dispositions, la DGE précise ainsi le cadre financier applicable aux candidats aux prochaines élections sénatoriales, tant pour le dépôt de la caution que pour la gestion et le contrôle des dépenses de campagne.

items.title: Curfew imposed in parts of central Paris and other cities after rioting across France
items.description: French authorities have imposed overnight curfews in parts of central Paris and other cities after a weekend of riots and looting across the country. Police in Paris said a curfew would be in force between 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) and 06:00 in Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area. A ban on unauthorised gatherings has also been imposed in several other parts of the city centre. Partial curfews, variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings, were announced for cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice, and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north. Earlier, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who has been strongly criticised by opposition politicians over the preparedness for the disorder but whose resignation was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron, admitted police had “lost control” in some cities. The protests began last month with students demanding better school conditions, but they have since expanded to encompass a broader range of concerns, with numbers at demonstrations this weekend bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups. More than 2,500 people have been arrested, officials said. One demonstrator’s hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured. Following a crisis meeting on Monday, the prime minister said local mayors were being given the power to implement curfews “where they need”, without specifying which cities where they would be enforced. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who did not rule out imposing a state of emergency in the country, said the government would also set aside funds to help affected areas recover from the damage, and that the costs would be recovered from those behind the violence. “There will be a law that will be put in place to find ways of making sure that those who have damaged properties will have to pay,” Lecornu said. He also announced a partial unemployment fund for those who could not work due to the riots and looting. French police officers check a person during a partial curfew in Lyon Meanwhile, Nuñez said 200 investigators were analysing CCTV footage to try to identify possible ringleaders. He attempted to resign on Sunday, but Macron refused “given the need for continued command of law enforcement”, the Élysée Palace said. The statement said Nuñez should be transparent about what Macron called “intelligence and foresight failings”. More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend’s violence, the head of France’s Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) says. Its head, Alain Di Crescenzo, told France’s broadcaster RTL that damage from the riots was estimated at “hundreds of millions of euros”. Jean-Luc Chauvin, the president of the CCI’s Marseille branch, told the BBC that many of the city’s shop owners were in “deep distress” and fear for their survival. Looted goods have been listed on certain selling platforms, two French government ministers said. A Vinted spokesperson said the sale or solicitation of stolen goods was “strictly prohibited”. “Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings,” it said. Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets over the weekend for protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools. Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns. In the central city of Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing as the flames took hold. The US Embassy in France has issued an alert advising its citizens to avoid areas affected by the recent demonstrations. The warning says to “exercise caution” if they find themselves close to large gatherings. China and Germany have issued similar warnings. Some politicians have accused the left-wing La France Insoumise party of playing a role in the violence, with Lecornu alleging in an earlier news conference that some groups “want to create chaos in our country up until the presidential elections”. The party’s leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who will stand in next year’s presidential election, responded by calling for the French PM to “prove his accusation” or “apologise, shut up, and stop stoking disorder”.

items.title: ‘We cannot yet quantify jobs created’ – 24-hour economy secretariat
items.description: The Chief Programme Officer of the 24-hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Secretariat, Abdul-Nasser Suglo Alidu, says he is unable to provide a total figure for jobs created under the government’s flagship policy. He said the government is working with the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) to establish a system to accurately measure the policy’s employment impact. Speaking on Joy FM’s Top Story on Monday, October 19, he said the Secretariat did not want to announce figures without reliable data. “Now, first of all, I won’t be able to give you a number in terms of the total number of jobs the 24-hour economy created. We don’t want to throw numbers around,” he said, explaining that structures were being put in place to capture the number of jobs generated across the economy when asked how many jobs has the 24-hour economy has created. His comments come amid questions about the policy’s progress, particularly its job creation targets. In 2024, proponents of the policy projected that it would absorb at least 300,000 people entering the workforce annually and reduce unemployment by 120,000 each year. However, Mr Suglo Alidu acknowledged that the Secretariat could not yet provide a nationwide figure to show how many jobs had been created since implementation began. He argued that although measures to stimulate job creation were being implemented, the systems needed to track their overall impact were not yet fully in place. Mr Suglo Alidu also pointed to increased credit to the private sector, citing a Bank of Ghana Monetary Policy Committee report, as an indication that businesses were gaining greater access to financing to support their activities and potentially employ more people. He stressed that the 24-hour economy policy went beyond getting businesses to operate in three shifts, describing it as a broader strategy to transform the economy and build globally competitive companies. He said, “several state enterprises and private businesses were already operating multiple shifts as part of efforts to extend economic activity beyond conventional working hours.”

items.title: ‘We have stabilised the present, now we must secure the future’ — Finance Minister
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson has called for a decisive break with the economic patterns that have held Ghana back, saying the country must now build on stabilisation to secure lasting prosperity. Speaking during his New Economy engagement with faculty and students at the University of Ghana, Dr Forson said Ghana had reached a moment when public policy must confront the underlying causes of its economic challenges. “We have stabilised the present. Now we must secure the future,” he declared. The Finance Minister framed the next phase of Ghana’s economic journey as a test of the country’s willingness to make decisions that would shape the prospects of future generations. “History does not wait for countries that are afraid to decide,” he said. “There are moments when a nation must make a clear break with old patterns. There are moments when public policy must stop managing symptoms and start changing structures. This is such a moment for Ghana.” His remarks placed structural transformation at the centre of the New Economy agenda, with economic stability serving as the foundation for a more productive economy that creates decent jobs and raises incomes. The challenge, he indicated, is to move beyond addressing immediate pressures and change the conditions that allow those pressures to recur. That ambition, to him, means producing more at home, adding value to what Ghana grows and mines, and expanding opportunities for businesses and workers.

items.title: Targeted interventions helping to reduce maternal deaths by 30 per cent at KATH – Deputy Health Minister
items.description: The Deputy Minister of Health, Dr Grace Ayensu-Danquah, has said targeted interventions have helped the Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital (KATH) in Kumasi for instance to reduce maternal deaths by 30 per cent in recent months. She attributed the reduction to a mentorship programme for doctors performing caesarean sections at lower-level health facilities and a virtual labour room through which specialists guided midwives remotely. Dr Ayensu-Danquah said the Ministry wanted the interventions adopted nationwide under a common plan to improve maternal healthcare. Speaking during a meeting of Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee (PAC) on Monday, October 19, 2026, Dr Ayensu-Danquah said a total of 445 maternal deaths had been recorded in Ghana by mid-year 2026, compared to a total of 419 during the same period in 2025. According to her, the slight increase is why the Ministry of Health has called for dedicated budget funding and National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) coverage for pregnant women’s critical care. She described maternal mortality as Ghana’s worst-performing health indicator, with the national rate standing at 234 deaths per 100,000 live births, more than three times the World Health Organisation (WHO) target of 70 deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030. “Behind every number is a woman, a family,” Dr Ayensu-Danquah told the committee. She said the Ministry has identified three major challenges contributing to maternal deaths. They include the failure to identify high-risk women, particularly those with hypertension or severe anaemia, at the primary healthcare level, delays and breakdowns in the referral and ambulance system, and shortages of blood, ventilators and intensive care facilities at secondary and tertiary hospitals. Dr Ayensu-Danquah said delays in accessing emergency care often determined whether a woman survived before she reached a teaching hospital. “In critical care we speak of the golden hour, the first 60 minutes after injury. If a woman waits 48 hours for an ambulance at the primary level, the outcome is already decided,” she said. She identified early detection of anaemia as one of the measures needed to reduce maternal deaths. She also urged health workers to recognise pica, a condition characterised by cravings for non-food items such as chalk or ice, as a possible sign of an underlying health problem. Dr Ayensu-Danquah further stressed the need for high-risk pregnant women to deliver at facilities equipped to manage complications rather than at Community-based Health Planning and Services (CHPS) compounds without the required capacity. Ahead of the 2027 Budget, the Ministry is seeking a dedicated budget allocation for maternal health to address what it describes as fragmented funding from non-governmental organisations and development partners. It is also pushing for the NHIS to cover critical care for pregnant women, including intensive care, oxygen, blood and specialist interventions. Interventions The Chairperson of the Public Accounts Committee, Abena Osei-Asare, said the committee would present the Auditor-General’s performance audit report on maternal mortality when Parliament resumed sitting. She said the report’s recommendations would inform discussions on the national budget. “We will support the Ministry in speaking to the Finance Minister to ensure some dedicated level of funding is given to maternal mortality healthcare in this country,” she said. Dr Ayensu-Danquah warned that without further action, Ghana risked maintaining a high maternal mortality rate beyond 2030. Ghana news platform “If we don’t do this, we will still be at 200-and-something in 2030. Our women are needlessly dying. Most of these deaths are preventable,” she said.

items.title: Customs to review complaints of 397 rejected recruitment applicants
items.description: By Efe Onodjae The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) has announced plans to review complaints by applicants who were disqualified during its recent recruitment screening exercise despite appearing on the shortlist for training. The Service said the Comptroller-General of Customs, Bashir Adewale Adeniyi, ordered a case-by-case review after meeting with some of the aggrieved applicants. In a statement signed by the National Public Relations Officer of the NCS, Deputy Comptroller of Customs Abdullahi Maiwada, on Monday, the NCS said the review was aimed at ensuring that legitimate complaints were examined while maintaining the integrity of the recruitment process. It explained that appearing on the final shortlist did not automatically guarantee enlistment, as applicants were required to undergo several stages of verification, including credential checks, physical fitness assessments, medical examinations, age verification and drug screening. According to the Service, screening irregularities involving 397 applicants were identified in areas including substance use, physical fitness, medical records, age and submitted documentation. It added that some candidates were also disqualified over irregularities identified in their selection process. The NCS urged affected applicants who believe they were unfairly disqualified to submit their details and complaints to helpdesk@customs.gov.ng for review. It said applicants seeking reconsideration would be subjected to fresh screening, stressing that the review would not automatically guarantee admission into the training college. The Service further warned that applicants found to have engaged in criminal conduct, including certificate fraud and other offences, would be referred for appropriate legal action and prosecution. It urged the affected candidates and the general public to remain calm and use the designated channel to submit their complaints. The post Customs to review complaints of 397 rejected recruitment applicants appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Samir Belfkih : le programme gouvernemental place les catégories sociales vulnérables au cœur des priorités
items.description: Le ministre de l’Aménagement du territoire national, de l’Urbanisme, de l’Habitat et de la Politique de la ville, porte-parole du gouvernement, Samir Belfkih, a assuré que le programme gouvernemental présenté lundi par la cheffe du gouvernement, Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, devant les deux Chambres du Parlement, repose sur une vision politique et une ambition commune : servir le Maroc et les Marocains et répondre à leurs attentes, notamment celles des jeunes, des habitants du monde rural et des différentes catégories de la société. Dans une déclaration à Hespress après la séance plénière des deux Chambres du Parlement, Belfkih a souligné que le programme accompagne les grands chantiers engagés par le Royaume en vue de son intégration effective et avancée au sein du club des pays émergents. Il repose également, a-t-il dit, sur une vision intégrée visant à répondre aux besoins des différentes catégories de la société, notamment les habitants des régions éloignées, les jeunes, les femmes et les veuves. Le porte-parole du gouvernement, qui s’est exprimé pour la deuxième fois officiellement depuis sa nomination à ce poste ministériel par le Roi Mohammed VI vendredi dernier, a indiqué que le principe général du document qui encadrera l’action gouvernementale durant le mandat de cinq ans est qu’aucun citoyen ne doit rester en marge et que chacun doit trouver sa place dans cette vision. Le système de l’éducation et de la formation occupe lui aussi une place importante dans ces orientations, a-t-il encore rappelé. L'objectif est qu’aucun élève ne reste en marge du système éducatif, a-t-il noté, évoquant la volonté de mettre fin à l’hémorragie du décrochage scolaire en apportant, à l’horizon 2031, une solution à la situation d’environ 300.000 élèves qui quittent chaque année l’école. Il a également cité l’objectif de permettre à 80 % des élèves d’acquérir les compétences nécessaires, afin d’obtenir des résultats différents des statistiques et des performances actuelles. Belfkih a poursuivi en expliquant que le programme s’inscrit dans une vision d’un « Maroc pour tous » et d’un « Maroc de l’égalité des chances ». Le citoyen vivant loin des centres urbains doit bénéficier des mêmes possibilités de promotion sociale qu’un jeune homme ou une jeune femme résidant dans la capitale ou dans les grandes villes, et « cette orientation traduit la volonté de rendre les possibilités de promotion accessibles à l’ensemble des citoyens, indépendamment de leur lieu de résidence », a-t-il estimé. Concernant la réponse aux attentes immédiates, le responsable gouvernemental a indiqué que le programme prévoit des mesures visant à améliorer le pouvoir d’achat des Marocains, notamment une réforme progressive de l’impôt sur le revenu. Il a également annoncé l’exonération, à partir de janvier 2027, des ménages dont la facture d’électricité est inférieure à 100 dirhams, sans qu’ils aient besoin de se déplacer à l’administration ou d’accomplir d’autres démarches. © Mounir Mehimdate Belfkih a par ailleurs évoqué une orientation visant à mettre fin aux intermédiaires entre producteurs et consommateurs. Il a, de même, abordé les engagements en matière de lutte contre la corruption, qui constituent un axe majeur du programme gouvernemental, précisant que celui-ci prévoit un chantier consacré à la criminalisation de l’enrichissement illicite. « Ce sujet figurait parmi les grandes attentes des Marocains », a-t-il dit. En outre, le dirigeant du Parti authenticité et modernité (PAM) a affirmé que la défense de ce programme et la lutte pour sa réalisation « se sont poursuivies jusqu’à ce que l’occasion se présente de travailler à sa mise en œuvre et de le traduire en mesures concrètes sur le terrain ». Il a enfin indiqué que le programme gouvernemental vise à valoriser les acquis, à corriger les dysfonctionnements et à répondre aux attentes des Marocains, en accordant une attention particulière aux jeunes, aux habitants du monde rural et aux catégories vulnérables qui ont besoin d’un soutien important de la part du gouvernement, dans le cadre d’une vision générale visant à servir les citoyens et à accompagner les grands chantiers engagés par le Royaume. The post Samir Belfkih : le programme gouvernemental place les catégories sociales vulnérables au cœur des priorités appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Keeping Ghana connected when fibre cables fail
items.description: When a mobile-money payment fails or a hospital cannot reach a referral team, the customer does not ask which fibre route is down. The immediate question is whether there is another way to complete an essential task. That should also be the starting point for Ghana’s approach to telecommunications resilience. On 26 September 2026, the National Communications Authority reported disruptions to voice and data services across the five northern regions and parts of Oti. Multiple fibre cuts had affected three transmission routes, disrupting or degrading 2G, 3G and 4G services. The Authority announced restoration the same day, following repairs by the National Information Technology Agency and network operators. The repair teams deserve credit. Their work should be followed by an equally serious examination of how essential communications can continue while damaged infrastructure is being restored. A second route must offer a different way through Imagine two roads linking a town to the rest of the country. If both cross the same bridge, a failure at that bridge can close both roads. Having two routes is useful only if the alternative survives the event that disables the first. Communications networks face a similar problem. Separate connections can occupy the same trench, cross the same bridge or depend on the same power supply. Buying services from different providers does not, by itself, establish that the underlying infrastructure is independent. This is a general engineering lesson, not a finding about the September incident. The NCA’s public notices do not establish the precise network layout, the causes of the cuts or who was responsible. Those questions require a technical investigation. What the disruption does justify is asking whether alternative routes can withstand shared risks. Preventing damage requires coordination beyond telecoms The NCA’s Communications Industry Report for 2023 recorded 751 fibre cuts across four reporting domestic fibre operators. It identified road construction, private development, utility work and fire among the main causes. These are historical figures, not a count of incidents this year. That record shows why the response must reach beyond network operators. Road agencies, local authorities, utilities and contractors need reliable information about buried infrastructure before excavation begins. A practical notification process, verified utility checks and clear emergency contacts can help prevent damage and speed up repairs. This need not mean publishing sensitive network maps. Detailed records should be available to authorised organisations under appropriate safeguards. The public needs assurance that coordination works, rather than a map of infrastructure vulnerabilities. Protect essential services during an outage A realistic resilience plan must say what remains available when capacity is reduced. Emergency coordination and selected health facilities may need protected minimum connectivity even when ordinary traffic cannot run at its usual speed. Hospitals and other critical institutions should identify their essential communications and agree recovery arrangements with their providers. The technical answer will vary by location. Physically diverse fibre remains the high-capacity foundation. Microwave or satellite connections may provide useful backup for selected services, provided they have adequate capacity, dependable power and tested switching arrangements. They should not be presented as universal replacements for major fibre routes. Procurement should therefore ask a more demanding question than whether a supplier offers a backup link. Which failure can that link survive, how much traffic can it carry, and how quickly can users switch to it? A cheaper connection that shares the same point of failure may offer little additional protection. A backup arrangement needs to be demonstrated under controlled conditions. Scheduled exercises should establish whether traffic actually moves to the alternative path and whether essential services remain usable. They should also test how long backup power lasts and whether the people responsible can coordinate a response. The World Bank’s guidance on resilient telecommunications supports this risk-based approach, combining network design with monitoring, backups, emergency planning and incident reporting. Investment decisions should reflect local conditions and the consequences of failure. Installing every possible backup everywhere would be neither affordable nor necessary. Start with a focused assessment of northern connectivity I propose an NCA-led assessment, working with NITA, operators and the relevant infrastructure agencies, of the routes and facilities serving northern Ghana. It should establish where shared risks exist, what essential services can continue during major failures, and which improvements would deliver the greatest benefit for their cost. The outcome should be a prioritised plan with named responsibilities and completion dates. A public summary could report restoration performance, backup-testing progress and completion of corrective actions without exposing sensitive technical details. Institutions purchasing connectivity should use those lessons to strengthen their own continuity plans. The September repairs restored service. The next task is to reduce the consequences of the next failure. Ghana should judge progress by how reliably people can keep communicating and using essential services when a cable is cut. That is the assurance a digital economy needs. About the author Prof. Abdul-Rahman Ahmed is a Professor at the Department of Telecommunications Engineering at KNUST and Founder of Stratfound Consult, a Ghanaian advisory firm working across telecommunications, ICT, energy and digital transformation. The views expressed are his own.

items.title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
items.description: As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did. Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory. But MPs and public figures – backed by experts – have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter. And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised. Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta. Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack. He was briefed by federal police – whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate – and told the national broadcaster: “This wasn’t an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear.” Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets. Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country. In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs – and in some cases their children – have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP’s office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor’s car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised. Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be “shamed and stoned in the square” over a tax policy. According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of “harassing and threatening behaviour” against “high office holders” in the year to June: an increase on last year. “We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, ‘Not here’, but this has been happening now for well over a decade,” Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC. Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, “grifters” who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a “carcinogenic” online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic. But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds. “We’ve seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain – you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families – but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life. “This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum.” And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too. Mike Burgess, the head of Australia’s spy agency, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia. “Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack,” he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026. And the Federal Police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. “Grievance” is radicalising people. “They’re feeling distanced, they’re feeling alone, they’re looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose,” Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month. There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and – if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed – one of the greatest tenets of the nation’s political culture could now be at risk. It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas. Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night. “Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people,” he said. “I don’t want to see a political system in which you can’t have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums – that’s an important part of our democracy.”
