items.title: ‘Close up your borders’ – Trump blames French unrest on immigration
items.description: US President Donald Trump on Monday again blamed immigration for protests and violence that have rocked France in recent days, urging Europe and French President Emmanuel Macron to tighten borders. “What’s happening in France has to do with immigration, not schools, not anything,” Trump told reporters in Washington, echoing his comments from the day before. “It’s immigration, and I told President Emmanuel Macron, close up your borders.” Weekend demonstrations over soaring prices were held in Paris and other cities, degenerating into some of the worst street violence France has seen in recent years. Trump recounted a conversation with Macron, telling him “a long time ago, you’re making a big mistake in France. You’re letting everybody from the world come in. The whole world was coming in. “Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon,” the 80-year-old Republican added. “If Europe doesn’t close its borders and bring the criminals out, like the people that are protesting, Europe is finished.” Trump made combating illegal immigration a central pledge of his 2024 campaign, at times relying on false claims that played on racial fears. AFP The post ‘Close up your borders’ – Trump blames French unrest on immigration appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Spain’s rush to clear Ceuta migrant backlog raises rights concerns
items.description: When heavily pregnant Fatna and her disabled son arrived in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta during a chaotic mass border crossing on July 30, she hoped to be high on authorities’ list for help. Nearly three months later, with her newborn baby girl suffering ​from kidney problems, Fatna, 21, and her family urgently need to reach mainland Spain for specialist hospital treatment. However, travelling while her asylum claim is under review requires a permit that Spain’s socialist government – ordinarily a staunch advocate of immigration – has ‌been reluctant to grant to any of the thousands of migrants remaining in Ceuta. Some are still scattered on the streets or hiding in the rolling hills of the tiny 20-sq-km port city on Morocco’s northeast border. Unaccompanied minors evicted over the weekend from an industrial estate near the border with Morocco were documented in local media sleeping on the pavement in front of the police headquarters, waiting to be registered. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government is under pressure from the EU and an increasingly frustrated populace to sort out the crisis and faces a snap election on November 29. It is working on shortcuts for asylum applications with the intention of sending most people home, mainly to Morocco, on the basis of ​being economic migrants, not real asylum-seekers. That, NGOs fear, risks violating migrants’ rights. More than 20 interviews by Reuters with migrants, lawyers, NGOs, and security forces revealed that many of those who remain have clear grounds for asylum or humanitarian protection: from unaccompanied minors to LGBT ​Moroccans fearing imprisonment if deported and families like Fatna’s classified as vulnerable under EU law. Last week, eight charities including Oxfam and Amnesty International filed a complaint with Spain’s ombudsman, seen by Reuters, alleging “grave rights violations” in ⁠the tiny Ceuta enclave. They included the forced return of migrants from conflict-hit countries and denial of interpreters and legal assistance. Spokespeople for Spain’s central government, the interior ministry, the territorial policy ministry, and the migration ministry did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment on the mistreatment accusations. Sanchez, one of Europe’s few remaining ​left-leaning leaders, said last week that Spain was managing the flood of cases “responsibly, with a sense of solidarity and respecting migrants’ human rights”. “There are people who will truly be in enormous danger if they are returned to Morocco,” said Wendell Soares, coordinator of the Catholic migrant reception centre San Antonio ​, which has taken in Fatna’s family and dozens more vulnerable people, far beyond its usual capacity of seven. “When the word ‘immigrant’ is used, it creates a collective image, as if they were all the same. Every person has their own story.” DEPORTED WITHOUT EXPLANATION Spanish right-wing and far-right parties were already angry with Sanchez’s government for providing legal status to nearly 1 million irregular migrants earlier this year. They have cast July’s crossing as a deliberate invasion by Morocco – an accusation Morocco denies, opens new tab – and demanded that all migrants be returned, opens new tab . But despite plans for a new EU-wide procedure enabling accelerated deportations in future emergency scenarios, current rules require that migrants be assessed case-by-case. While most are from Morocco, the government estimated in August ​that more than 1,000 of the migrants remaining were from sub-Saharan countries whose nationals are granted asylum in over 90% of cases in Spain, according to government statistics. The EU’s new pact requires that cases be processed in border zones to permit faster deportations. But it does not require applicants to ​stay where they arrived, allowing for transfers to other border zones in Spain that would alleviate pressure on the 84,000-person enclave of Ceuta, Europe’s only land border with Africa. If vulnerable migrants’ cases are to be properly assessed, such transfers are the “only option”, said Juan Miguel Morales, director-general of NGO Sur Acoge. While 262 minors have ‌been transferred to the ⁠Spanish mainland since the July crossing, the government’s strategy for the remaining adults has been to convince as many as possible to return of their own volition. The government said this week that 12,000 had chosen to cross back since mid-August. “There are no covert deportations under any circumstances,” Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said, describing the returns as voluntary and adding that up to 1,200 asylum applications had been received and 700 of them resolved. However, at least nine NGOs have in public communication or interviews with Reuters claimed that migrants they support were coerced to return. Asociación Elin said migrants from Sudan and Chad were summoned by police on September 24 and 25 and deported without warning, according to the complaint to the ombudsman. In text messages reviewed by Reuters, Moroccan migrant Azhaar Chaouni told volunteers at German NGO Mission Lifeline that he and other migrants faced the same fate, after being picked up in buses by ​police from their makeshift camps on the beach and told they were ​being taken to reception centres. “They deported us without explanation,” Chaouni ⁠wrote, saying he was in Morocco. Morocco’s designation as a “safe country of origin” under EU rules does not strip its citizens of the right to apply for asylum, said Andrea de Petris, immigration expert at the think tank CEP, based in Freiburg, Germany. “Each individual must be guaranteed a specific assessment of their personal circumstances,” added De Petris who estimates the procedure would inevitably be “lengthy and costly”. Stories of others disappearing have instilled fear in Rayane, a 19-year-old gay Moroccan ​awaiting news on his asylum application in the San Antonio reception centre. Rejected by his family and unable to live openly in Morocco where same-sex sexual acts are prosecuted, he is desperate to get to ​mainland Europe. “I can’t even imagine myself going ⁠back to Morocco. I’d kill myself before even crossing the border,” he said. PACT EXPOSED Frontline workers and NGOs on the ground say the situation in Ceuta has proven that the 12-week limit set in the EU’s migrant pact for processing asylum applications is unrealistic, with seven stating they expect the process to drag on for months. A lack of resources from staff to functioning computers meant that only around 100 migrants’ cases were being registered daily by October 14, according to police union representative Raul Piera. The union estimates roughly 7,000-8,000 more migrants are still scattered across the city, sleeping rough or squeezed into facilities provided by charities and civil ⁠society groups filling the ​gap left by Ceuta’s overwhelmed social services. “Looking at the remaining workload, this will last well into next summer,” said Piera. Spain’s government has declined to comment on estimates of unregistered ​migrants, with Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres telling reporters on October 14 that it was impossible to know how many were hiding. Doctors in Ceuta’s only hospital are treating migrants for scabies, tuberculosis and gastrointestinal infections caused by long periods outdoors, said Enrique Robiralta, head of the doctors’ union. At least seven women have given birth. Fatna and her husband Mohamed are ​desperate to stay in Spain, fearing for the new baby and convinced their 3-year-old disabled son will die in Morocco. “We are doing everything for our son,” said Mohamed.

items.title: Problématique de la pollution plastique, de l’eau potable et des séismes : ce que prépare le gouvernement
items.description: Lutte contre la pollution plastique, renforcement de l’accès à l’eau potable et surveillance des secousses sismiques : le Gouvernement guinéen a précisé ses orientations sur ces trois enjeux lors d’une conférence de presse conjointe des porte-parole de la Présidence et du Gouvernement. Faya François Bourouno, ministre de la Fonction publique et porte-parole du Gouvernement, a notamment annoncé un moratoire de six mois pour accompagner les acteurs économiques dans la transition vers des alternatives aux plastiques concernés. La lutte contre la pollution plastique reste une priorité affichée des autorités guinéennes. Face aux difficultés liées à l’application des mesures de restriction, le Gouvernement entend privilégier une démarche progressive, conciliant impératifs environnementaux, réalités économiques et préservation des emplois. Lors de cette conférence de presse, François Bourouno a annoncé un moratoire de six mois, destiné à permettre aux industriels, aux commerçants et aux autres acteurs concernés de s’adapter aux nouvelles exigences et d’explorer des solutions de remplacement plus durables. Cette période transitoire ne constitue pas, selon le Gouvernement, un abandon de la politique engagée. Elle vise plutôt à faciliter sa mise en œuvre, tout en limitant les conséquences économiques et sociales de la transition et en préservant la continuité des services publics. Pollution plastique : une transition progressive Selon le porte-parole du Gouvernement, les premières mesures engagées auraient déjà contribué à une diminution importante des déchets plastiques visibles dans les espaces publics. Les autorités y voient un signe encourageant, qu’elles entendent consolider grâce à une mobilisation accrue des citoyens et des acteurs économiques. L’objectif est désormais d’accélérer l’évolution des habitudes de consommation et de réduire progressivement la dépendance aux plastiques à usage unique. Faya François Bourouno a salué l’implication des populations ainsi que les efforts des industriels et des commerçants engagés dans cette transition. Il a également invité les médias à renforcer les campagnes de sensibilisation afin de faire de la protection de l’environnement une responsabilité collective. Au-delà des restrictions, la gestion des déchets constitue un autre défi majeur pour les villes guinéennes. La collecte, le tri, le recyclage et la valorisation des déchets représentent autant de pistes pour améliorer l’assainissement du cadre de vie et favoriser l’émergence de nouvelles activités économiques. Ces initiatives pourraient également contribuer à la création d’emplois, notamment pour les jeunes et les petites entreprises, à condition que des mécanismes d’accompagnement et des investissements adaptés soient mis en place. Le défi consiste ainsi à concilier la protection de l’environnement, l’adaptation des pratiques industrielles et commerciales et la préservation des moyens de subsistance des acteurs concernés. Eau potable : plus de 600 millions d’euros annoncés Autre sujet abordé lors de cette rencontre avec la presse est l’amélioration des conditions d’accès à l’eau potable. Le ministre Bourouno a évoqué un projet d’envergure mobilisant un financement de plus de 600 millions d’euros pour renforcer les infrastructures hydrauliques du pays. Les interventions annoncées comprennent notamment la réhabilitation de 13 stations de traitement d’eau, des investissements dans plusieurs villes ainsi que la création de nouveaux points d’accès à l’eau potable. Ces investissements s’inscrivent dans la volonté des autorités d’améliorer les conditions de vie des populations et de renforcer l’accès aux services publics essentiels. Leur impact dépendra toutefois de la bonne exécution des travaux, de la couverture effective des localités ciblées et de la capacité à assurer durablement la production et la distribution de l’eau potable. La gestion des déchets plastiques et l’accès à l’eau apparaissent ainsi comme deux enjeux complémentaires de santé publique, d’assainissement et de développement durable. Secousses sismiques : les services techniques mobilisés La conférence de presse a également été l’occasion d’aborder les secousses sismiques récemment signalées dans certaines localités du pays. Sur cette question, le porte-parole du Gouvernement a indiqué que les services techniques de l’État avaient été mobilisés afin d’évaluer la situation et de prendre les dispositions nécessaires à la protection des populations. Il a appelé les citoyens au calme, tout en insistant sur l’importance de la prévention des risques et de la communication avec les communautés concernées. Dans ce contexte, le suivi technique des phénomènes signalés et la diffusion d’informations fiables restent essentiels pour éclairer les populations, prévenir les inquiétudes injustifiées et limiter la propagation de rumeurs. À travers ces différents sujets, le Gouvernement met en avant trois priorités : la transition vers des pratiques plus respectueuses de l’environnement, le renforcement des infrastructures d’eau potable et la vigilance face aux risques naturels. Leur concrétisation dépendra désormais de la mise en œuvre effective des mesures annoncées et de leur impact sur les conditions de vie des populations.

items.title: Maddison shines as Tottenham claim long-awaited first PL win of season
items.description: James Maddison made a sensational return to Tottenham’s starting line-up after 17 months away on Monday as Spurs beat Coventry 3-1 to claim their long-awaited first Premier League win of the season. The England midfielder has featured only fleetingly since May 2025, when he suffered the first of two serious knee injuries. But Maddison needed less than a quarter of an hour to put Spurs ahead at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium with a stunning first-time strike from outside the penalty area. Jack Rudoni levelled early in the second half but the home side were back in front just before the hour mark when Omar Marmoush lashed home his first goal for the club and substitute Ben Davies made the points safe late on. Roberto De Zerbi’s team came into the match bottom of the Premier League and with the unwanted record of being the only team in England’s top six divisions without a league win this season despite a huge summer spend. The Spurs boss had taken his squad to Marbella in southern Spain for some warm-weather training in a bid to kickstart their season. He named Maddison in his starting line-up while Sweden midfielder Dejan Kulusevski returned to the matchday squad for the first time in 17 months. Maddison ruptured the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee in August 2025, just three months after injuring the same knee. The 29-year-old wasted little time in making his mark, putting his side ahead in the 14th minute in spectacular style after fine work from Mohammed Kudus on the right. Maddison, lurking just outside the penalty area, received the ball from Kudus and sent it curling past Coventry goalkeeper Carl Rushworth and into the top corner, sparking wild scenes of delight among the home fans. Tottenham now had their tails up and threatened to overwhelm the visitors but Frank Lampard’s newly promoted Coventry, who had won their previous two games, re-established a foothold. Maddison went close to putting Spurs 2-0 after half an hour but his half-cross, half-shot curled narrowly wide. But they failed to stretch their lead and Coventry were level in the 49th minute, courtesy of a Rudoni strike from close range. Spurs lost the ball in the Coventry half and the visitors swept forward. Rudoni’s cross hit a teammate but the ball fell kindly for him and he drove home. Just nine minutes later Spurs were back in front when former Manchester City forward Marmoush held off Milan van Ewijk before unleashing an unstoppable shot. Kulusevski, who suffered a knee injury in May 2025, was introduced in the final minutes to a huge ovation from the home fans. Spurs veteran Davies made the three points safe deep into added time, poking home from the edge of the penalty area as Tottenham could at last relax. AFP The post Maddison shines as Tottenham claim long-awaited first PL win of season appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Le président Doumbouya crée la Société Nationale du Tabac (décret)
items.description: Dans un décret publié dans la soirée de ce lundi 19 octobre 2026 à la télévision nationale, le président Mamadi Doumbouya, a procédé à la création en Guinée de la Société Nationale du Tabac dénommée « S.N.T ». Titre I : Dispositions générales . Article 1 : Création — Il est créé sous la dénomination « Société nationale du tabac en abrégé S.N.T. » une société d'État dotée de la personnalité morale et de l'autonomie financière, chargée de la mise en œuvre du monopole de l'État sur le tabac institué par la loi N 2015 015 AN du 22 juillet 2015 et régie par les dispositions de l'acte uniforme relatif au droit des sociétés commerciales et du groupement d'intérêt économique de l'OHADA. . Article 2 : Siège — Le siège social de la Société nationale du tabac est fixé à Conakry. Il peut être transféré en tout autre lieu du territoire national par décision du conseil d'administration approuvée par les tutelles. . Article 3 : Durée — La durée de la SNT est de 99 ans, sauf en cas de dissolution anticipée ou de prorogation. . Article 4 : Objet — La SNT a pour objet l'exercice pour le compte de l'État du monopole défini à l'article 2 de la loi N 2015 015 AN portant sur : ​Le contrôle et la régularisation de la culture du tabac sur le territoire national. ​La commercialisation du tabac brut, l'importation comme l'exportation, la production et la transformation industrielle du tabac sur le territoire national, l'importation et l'exportation des produits finis du tabac. Titre II : Missions ​ Article 5 : Missions — Dans le cadre de son objet, la SNT est notamment chargée de : ​Instruire et proposer au ministre chargé du Commerce les autorisations et licences prévues par les textes d'application de la loi. ​Organiser l'achat du tabac brut auprès des producteurs directement ou par voie de convention avec des opérateurs agréés. ​Assurer la traçabilité du tabac du champ jusqu'à la mise sur le marché. ​Faire assurer le contrôle de la qualité du tabac et de ses produits finis par l'organe en charge du contrôle qualité. ​Constituer et gérer les stocks de sécurité et les stocks stratégiques. ​Représenter ou assister l'État dans les négociations accords internationaux relatifs au tabac. ​Concourir à liaison avec l'administration des douanes et les services du ministère du Commerce à lutter contre la fraude, la contrebande et la commercialisation non autorisée du tabac. ​Proposer aux tutelles toutes mesures de nature à améliorer l'exercice du monopole et à en accroître le rendement pour le Trésor public. Titre III : Organes ​ Article 6 : Organes de la SNT — La SNT est administrée par un conseil d'administration et dirigée par une direction générale. Son contrôle financier doit assurer sous les conditions fixées par la réglementation applicable aux sociétés d'État. ​ Article 7 : Composition du conseil d'administration — Le conseil d'administration est composé de neuf membres ainsi répartis : ​Un représentant de la présidence de la République. ​Deux représentants du ministère chargé de l'Industrie et du Commerce. ​Un représentant du ministère chargé des Finances. ​Un représentant du ministère chargé de l'Agriculture. ​Un représentant du ministère chargé de la Santé. ​Deux représentants des organisations professionnelles des producteurs de tabac légalement constitués désignés selon les modalités fixées par arrêté du ministre chargé du Commerce. ​Deux personnalités qualifiées désignées en raison de leur compétence dans le secteur du tabac, de l'agro-industrie ou de la gestion d'entreprise. Les membres du conseil d'administration sont nommés par décret du président de la République pour un mandat de trois ans renouvelable une seule fois. Un représentant du personnel de la SNT élu par ses pairs assiste aux conseils aux séances du conseil avec voix consultative. ​ Article 8 : Fonctionnement du conseil d'administration — Le conseil d'administration se réunit en session ordinaire une fois par trimestre sur convocation de son président et en session extraordinaire chaque fois que nécessaire à l'initiative de son président, du directeur général ou des tiers au moins des membres. Il ne délibère valablement que si la majorité absolue de ses membres est présente ou représentée. Les décisions sont prises à la majorité simple des membres présents ou représentés. En cas de partage égal des voix, celle du président est prépondérante. Les membres du conseil d'administration perçoivent des indemnités de session dont le montant est fixé par arrêté conjoint du ministre chargé du Commerce et du ministre chargé des Finances. ​ Article 9 : Attributions du conseil d'administration — Le conseil d'administration délibère notamment sur le budget et les états financiers, le plan d'activité, l'organigramme, les conventions avec les opérateurs privés du secteur ainsi que pour toutes propositions de textes réglementaires relatifs à l'exercice du monopole… L’article Le président Doumbouya crée la Société Nationale du Tabac (décret) est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Why is Obuasi SHTS headmaster still on NFA Board? – Juliet Asante asks
items.description: Ghanaian filmmaker and former National Film Authority (NFA) Executive Secretary Juliet Yaa Asantewaa Asante has questioned why Zakaria Abdulai, headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), remains on the Authority’s Governing Board despite allegations of sexual misconduct involving female students. In a Facebook post shared on Monday, 19th October 2026, alongside a picture of Mr. Abdulai, Juliet asked: “Why is this gentleman still on the board of the National Film Authority? “Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts, please tell us. #YaaMusings #JulietAsante. There is really no art to find the mind’s construction on the face…” Four days earlier, Juliet had published a lengthy statement on Facebook titled “THE NATIONAL FILM AUTHORITY MUST SPEAK”, raising concerns about Mr Abdulai’s continued membership of the NFA board and calling for the Authority to address the matter publicly. “I have followed with deep concern the disturbing reports surrounding Zakaria Abdulai, headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School, and the serious allegations of sexual misconduct involving female students currently under investigation,” she wrote. “The reports are deeply troubling, particularly given the number of students who have reportedly come forward and the questions being raised about how earlier complaints were handled.” She said Mr Abdulai’s membership of the NFA board made the matter particularly concerning to her. “He served on the Authority’s board during my tenure as its founding CEO, representing the Film Producers’ Association of Ghana, and was subsequently reappointed to the board inaugurated in August 2025, this time representing the Collective Management Organisation of Audiovisual Rights Owners. “His association with the governance of the NFA therefore spans two board appointments.” As the founding CEO of the institution, she said the developments were deeply disturbing. “But beyond my personal concern lies a much bigger question. “What responsibility does a public institution have when one of its governing board members becomes the subject of allegations of this magnitude?” The Ghana Education Service (GES) has interdicted Mr Abdulai pending investigations into the allegations. The Minister of Education, Haruna Iddrisu, also directed his suspension and requested the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) headquarters of the Ghana Police Service to investigate the matter. However, Juliet Asante noted that the NFA had issued no public statement addressing Mr Abdulai’s position on its governing board or the implications of the developments for the institution. “Institutional silence in the face of allegations of this magnitude raises serious questions about accountability and public trust. “The NFA owes the public and the audiovisual filmmaking community a clear response.” She called on the Authority to affirm its commitment to ethical leadership and institutional integrity, clarify Mr Abdulai’s current board status, and explain the measures being taken or considered pending the outcome of investigations. “Respecting due process does not absolve public institutions of their responsibility to demonstrate accountability,” she said. Juliet also raised concerns about appointments to the boards of public institutions, questioning the background checks and due diligence undertaken before individuals are appointed, the ethical standards applied, and the mechanisms available to assess the continued suitability of board members when serious concerns arise. “These are not ceremonial positions. Board members exercise oversight, influence policy, shape institutional direction and carry the responsibility of protecting the public interest. “The National Film Authority is entrusted with the development, regulation and promotion of Ghana’s film industry. It carries responsibilities that extend across our audiovisual and creative economy. Its governance must reflect the highest standards of integrity, accountability and public trust.” She called on the NFA, its supervising ministry, the Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts, and the relevant appointing authorities to address the matter publicly, take appropriate action in accordance with the law, and strengthen the vetting and accountability mechanisms governing appointments to public boards. “Above all, the young people at the centre of these allegations deserve protection, dignity, a thorough and independent investigation, and justice wherever wrongdoing is established. “The institutions we build must be protected by standards greater than the individuals appointed to govern them. “Public trust is not maintained through silence. It is maintained through accountability.” NFA board membership The current governing board of the National Film Authority was inaugurated on Monday, 4th August 2025, in Accra. Mr Abdulai represents the Collective Management Organisation of Audio Visual Rights Owners (ARSOG) on the board. He also served on the NFA board under the previous government. President Nana Akufo-Addo inaugurated the first NFA board on 20th December 2019, with veteran actor David Dontoh as chairperson. Mr Abdulai represented the Film Producers Association of Ghana (FIPAG) at the time. He was retained on the board inaugurated in October 2021. The NFA’s mandate is established under Ghana’s Development and Classification of Film Act, 2016 (Act 935). Its main responsibility is to regulate, develop and promote Ghana’s film industry. Allegations against headmaster Mr Abdulai has come under scrutiny following a JoyNews investigation by journalist Manasseh Azure Awuni into allegations of sexual harassment, assault and rape involving female students. The documentary, Inside the Dreaded Headmaster’s Bungalow , also examined how authorities handled complaints against him. On 13h October 2026, Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu directed the Ghana Education Service to suspend Mr Abdulai pending a full investigation. The minister also requested the CID headquarters to investigate the allegations. The documentary found that students, parents and teachers had submitted complaints to school management, education officials and other authorities before the suspension. The allegations remain under investigation.

items.title: Italian police detain hundreds as stores looted in weekend unrest in Milan
items.description: Italian police detained 271 young people during unrest in Milan on Sunday, authorities said, ​after a second day of protests over poor ‌public services and rising costs that saw demonstrators clash with officers, loot stores and vandalise property. Police in riot ​gear fired tear gas and water cannon as ​several hundred hooded protesters set bins ablaze ⁠and looted stores including sports retailers Decathlon and ​Arc’teryx and phone store Vodafone in the city centre, according ​to TV footage. Of those taken to police stations, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, police ​said on Monday. A further 28 people were ​reported to judicial authorities. The unrest followed similar clashes on Saturday in ‌northern ⁠cities including Milan, Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, according to a police report released on Sunday. The disturbances echoed unrest in neighbouring ​France , where ​hundreds of ⁠thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took ​to the streets on Saturday in ​some of ⁠the country’s most violent protests in years. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who faces an election next year, ⁠condemned ​the violence and announced a ​government meeting on Monday to discuss how to address the situation.

items.title: What Trump’s Comments About France Say About Him
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. You might imagine that, given the imminent midterm elections, a spluttering war in Iran, and his sinking personal approval , Donald Trump has enough to worry about. Not so. The president has been posting prolifically on Truth Social over the past two days about protests in France. “The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!” he wrote this morning . Trump’s reactions don’t tell us a great deal about the protests or about French society, but they do reveal three things about Trump. First, Trump’s favorite mode is punditry. Even as the world’s most powerful man, he frequently seems to prefer watching TV and shooting opinions from the hip to engaging in governance. This explains why he continued to give freewheeling briefings, full of his own speculation and medical advice, while the coronavirus swept the United States in 2020, and it might be one reason he’s fixated on France at a time of political peril for his own party. Second, and related, Trump can’t resist meddling in other countries’ affairs, engaging in behavior that previous presidents would have concluded was inappropriate. The U.S. government has long worked to covertly influence foreign elections, and in some cases encouraged or fomented coups. But presidents have mostly avoided issuing public endorsements or other interventions in partisan politics overseas, two things Trump loves to do. He endorsed the prime minister of Japan for reelection, backed a right-wing candidate for president of Poland, placed tariffs on Brazil for prosecuting his ally Jair Bolsonaro, and lent his administration’s credibility to the reelection campaign of Hungary’s then-President Viktor Orbán. (Orbán lost.) This weekend, he endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump’s blaming of immigrants in France amplifies the platform of National Rally, a far-right party with fascist roots that is ideologically aligned with MAGA and has its best shot yet at capturing the French presidency for the first time next spring. But U.S. interference abroad tends to produce some pushback. Leaders and voters in sovereign countries may not like a superpower telling them how to live—especially in a nation such as France, which still sees itself as a global player. Apologists might contend that Trump’s meddling in foreign politics is a sign of strength, projecting American power worldwide, but the brush-off Trump received when begging for international assistance in the Persian Gulf showed the cost of treating allies dismissively. Trump’s approach to the protests is notable because for years, he seemed to get along with French President Emmanuel Macron better than with almost any other foreign leader, a bromance sealed with history’s most awkward handshake . Their friendship seems to have cooled more recently, in part because of tariffs and Trump’s antagonism toward Ukraine . (Notably, the Kremlin is also using France’s protests to score political points.) Third, Trump views all forms of protest—at least those with which he disagrees—as inherently illegitimate. The violence in France warrants concern: This past weekend, the country saw some of its worst riots in decades; shops were looted and landmarks were destroyed as rioters seemed to take advantage of the mass marches. But in his posts on Truth Social, the president does not simply condemn the violence—he suggests that the riots must be the work of foreign seditionists . The protest movement was in fact sparked by domestic concerns, particularly demands for better funding for the nation’s school system. Macron, in contrast to Trump, has said that many protestors have legitimate demands, even as he has fiercely condemned violence, which he blames on “troublemakers from far-left fringe groups.” Authoritarians see any popular resistance as a danger to their power, which is why the autocratic Russian regime and the aspiring strongman Trump are united in condemning French demonstrations. And as nationalists, they must also blame the danger on outsiders, even though French authorities have not made any link between immigrants and unrest. “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion,” Vice President Vance posted on X this weekend, along with a clip of the city hall in Limoges, in the old province of Limousin, burning. “They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn’t listen.” This was not only a missed opportunity for Vance to blame literal limousine liberals for the riots; it was patently absurd. The French don’t need outsiders to teach them how to rage in the streets. They’ve been doing it for centuries. (Trump, an aficionado of Les Misérables , might not have made this mistake .) To the extent that migrants are involved in these protests, it is proof that they have assimilated fully to the French way of life. Suggesting that Trump and Vance might be wiser to focus on getting their own house in order than to look overseas would be easy, but it misses the point. This weekend, while Trump was posting about French protests, Americans were participating in thousands of “No Kings” demonstrations around the country and Trump’s “border czar” was insinuating that Ilhan Omar, a Democratic lawmaker who is a naturalized citizen, committed immigration fraud. Trump’s attempts to delegitimize protest and whip up xenophobia aren’t ultimately about France. They’re about the United States. Related: Why Trump turned to the sewer ( From 2025 ) The violence sweeping France was never really about schools. Here are four new stories from The Atlantic : Leo J. Wise: How corruption got this bad Tom Nichols: America is now an ally of Russia. Maine has changed. Susan Collins hasn’t. Jonathan Chait: Mamdani is the centrist we’ve been waiting for. Today’s News The Supreme Court rejected an appeal by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other accused September 11 plotters who are seeking to reinstate a 2024 plea deal that would have given them life sentences. The three men are scheduled to stand trial before a military commission in 2028 and could face the death penalty. Yesterday, President Trump defended his decision to ease sanctions and tariffs on Russia , saying the move was intended to keep Moscow at the negotiating table for a peace agreement with Ukraine. He also suggested that the talks included negotiations over the release of a hostage, but he did not identify anyone involved. Houthi forces launched three ballistic missiles at a military camp in Yemen’s Shabwa province, killing at least 47 people and injuring at least 53 others, according to Yemeni military officials. The attack comes amid renewed fighting between the Iran-backed group and Yemeni government forces supported by Saudi Arabia. Dispatches The Wonder Reader : Rafaela Jinich explores how to indulge in fall . Explore all of our newsletters here. Evening Read Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic The Minimal Requirements for a Society Free From Fear By Adam Kirsch In 1989, the year the West won the Cold War, Francis Fukuyama published an essay announcing “the end of history.” He wasn’t claiming that historic events would stop taking place; what was over, rather, was the debate about the meaning of those events. Since the Enlightenment, Western thinkers had believed that history was progressing toward a final destination. According to communism, the engine of progress was class conflict, and history would end in the creation of a classless society. With the failure of the Soviet empire, Fukuyama argued, this idea had been discredited. Only one alternative remained: It was now clear that the “end point of mankind’s ideological evolution” was “the universalization of Western liberal democracy as the final form of human government.” There would still be disagreements within liberalism—Fukuyama named religion and nationalism as likely fault lines—but there could no longer be any disagreement about liberalism. items.title: Florida issues arrest warrant for Cuba’s ex-leader Raul Castro
items.description: Florida’s top prosecutor announced an arrest warrant Monday for former Cuban president Raul Castro on state murder charges that echo a federal indictment unveiled earlier this year. Raul Castro, 95, is wanted on murder charges connected to the February 24, 1996 shooting down of two civilian aircraft from “Brothers to the Rescue,” an organization assisting Cubans fleeing to the US state by sea. “Raul Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy,” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said in a statement. Castro, brother of the late revolutionary leader and US nemesis Fidel Castro, was indicted on federal charges related to the incident in May. The move came as President Donald Trump’s right-wing administration steadily ramped up economic, political and legal pressure on the Cuban communist government. “We’re committed to pursuing every lawful, prosecutable avenue to bring accountability, including parallel federal and state prosecutions,” US Attorney Jason A. Reding Quinones said in a statement supporting Florida’s action. “We’re proud to stand with Florida in seeking justice for the four Americans murdered in the Brothers to the Rescue shootdown nearly 30 years ago,” the federal prosecutor said. In a statement on X, Cuba’s Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez condemned “the latest futile maneuver by anti-Cuban politicians in South Florida,” which he said was a “reflection of political rot and moral collapse.” Trump previously seized on a US indictment to justify military action in January that toppled Venezuela’s then-president Nicolas Maduro, a staunch ally of the Cuban authorities. Current Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel has said the US federal indictment against Castro has “no legal basis” and was an attempt “to justify the folly of a military aggression against Cuba.” AFP The post Florida issues arrest warrant for Cuba’s ex-leader Raul Castro appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: IPOB urges Britain to press Nigeria for Nnamdi Kanu’s appeal
items.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru The Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) has urged the British Government to use its diplomatic channels to press Nigeria to hear the pending appeal of its leader, Mazie Nnamdi Kanu, without further delay. In a statement on Monday signed by its spokesperson, Emma Powerful, IPOB said the British Government should engage Nigerian authorities over the delay in the hearing of Kanu’s appeal and other related cases. The group questioned Britain’s response to Kanu’s legal situation, arguing that its stated policy of assisting British nationals detained abroad when internationally accepted standards are not met should inform its engagement with Nigeria. IPOB asked the British Government to explain how Kanu’s treatment aligns with international standards on legality, due process and fundamental human rights. The group raised five issues, including Kanu’s rendition from Kenya to Nigeria in June 2021, the Court of Appeal’s judgment of October 13, 2022, his conviction in November 2025, the status of some charges and the delay in hearing his appeal. On his rendition, IPOB cited Opinion No. 25/2022 of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, which it said called for Kanu’s immediate release. It also questioned the subsequent proceedings against him in light of the Court of Appeal’s judgment, which discharged him on specified counts. The group further challenged the legal basis of Kanu’s conviction, arguing that the terrorism legislation underlying the charges had been repealed. It cited Section 36(12) of the Nigerian Constitution, which provides that a person cannot be convicted of a criminal offence unless the offence and its penalty are prescribed in a written law. IPOB also questioned the inclusion of counts it said had previously been discharged by the Court of Appeal, arguing that the issues required clarification in the ongoing legal process. On the delayed appeal, the group urged Britain to make representations to the Nigerian Government to ensure that the case is heard promptly. IPOB maintained that diplomatic representations over due process, human rights and delays in judicial proceedings would not amount to interference in Nigeria’s judicial independence. It said it was not asking Britain to dictate the outcome of the case but to use its diplomatic engagement to encourage the timely hearing of Kanu’s appeal. The group called on the British Government to press Nigeria to list and hear the appeal, alongside related cases before the relevant courts, without further delay. Kanu was convicted on terrorism-related charges in November 2025 and sentenced to life imprisonment. His legal team has challenged his conviction. IPOB said the British Government should demonstrate its commitment to protecting its citizens by seeking a prompt hearing of the pending appeal. The post IPOB urges Britain to press Nigeria for Nnamdi Kanu’s appeal appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Natural resources, the environment and the Constitutional Review Committee’s recommendations: Why government should reconsider its position
items.description: The publication of Government’s Position Paper on the Final Recommendations of the Constitution Review Committee (CRC) has brought some clarity to Ghana’s latest constitutional reform exercise. Government accepts the need for constitutional reform but takes the view, quite properly, that not every desirable policy or administrative arrangement belongs in the Constitution. That caution is understandable because a constitution should state enduring principles of governance and leave matters of detail to legislation. The difficulty, however, is that Government appears to have carried this principle too far in its treatment of the final recommendations of the CRC on the lands, natural resources and environmental thematic areas. The CRC proposed, among other things, a clearer public trust framework for natural resources, stronger parliamentary oversight of resource transactions, basic principles for natural resource governance, improved institutional coordination, constitutional recognition of ocean governance and the blue economy, the creation of an offence of ecocide, and a guaranteed share of mineral revenue for mining communities. 1 Government has declined substantially all these proposals. Its recurring justification is that the existing constitutional provisions are adequate or that the objectives can be achieved through ordinary legislation, including the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703), the Fisheries Act, 2002 (Act 625), the Petroleum Revenue Management Act, 2011 (Act 815), and the Environmental Protection Act, 2025 (Act 1124). 2 The difference between the CRC and Government is therefore not entirely about the desirability of better natural resource and environmental governance. It is principally about where the governing principles should reside. And that distinction deserves closer scrutiny. Natural Resources Are Already a Constitutional Question The starting point is the 1992 Constitution itself. Article 257(1) vests public lands in the President on behalf of, and in trust for, the people of Ghana. Article 257(6) similarly vests every mineral in its natural state in, under or upon land in Ghana, rivers, streams and watercourses, as well as the territorial sea, continental shelf and exclusive economic zone, in the President on behalf of, and in trust for, the people. 3 Article 268 goes further by stating that transactions involving the grant of rights or concessions for the exploitation of Ghana’s mineral, water or other natural resources are made subject to parliamentary ratification. Article 269, in turn, provides for commissions responsible for regulating and managing the utilisation of natural resources and coordinating policy concerning them. 4 The framers, therefore, made a deliberate choice when they considered natural resources too important to be left entirely to ordinary legislation. Consequently, the proper question to be answered is whether more than three decades of experience under the 1992 Constitution justify improving the constitutional principles by which those resources are governed. The author, Anthony Danquah, Esq. Government answers largely in the negative. In relation to public lands, it reasons that the present vesting in the President is already fiduciary and that the President holds no personal interest in those lands. It further considers the Lands Act, 2020 (Act 1036) adequate to deal with fiduciary obligations, compensation, reversionary interests and compulsory acquisition. 5 The first proposition may be accepted without accepting the second in that if the President already holds public lands and natural resources as trustee for the people, there is every reason for the Constitution to state with greater clarity what that trusteeship requires. Here, the language of Article 257 is important. The President holds the relevant resources “on behalf of, and in trust for” the people. Trusteeship ordinarily carries obligations. It is therefore insufficient to identify the trustee and the trust property without asking what duties accompany the trust, in whose interests they must be exercised and how breaches of those duties are to be addressed. This difficulty in the present constitutional arrangement was elucidated by Rameau and Bamba in their examination of the fiduciary role of Government under the 1992 Constitution. They revisited the Supreme Court’s decision in Adjaye v. Attorney-General and questioned the conception of the constitutional trust as lacking the incidents of an enforceable fiduciary relationship. 6 Their argument is particularly relevant to the present constitutional review because it exposes the uncertainty surrounding the practical meaning of the trust created by Article 257. The CRC proposal offered an opportunity to remove some of the uncertainty. At a minimum, constitutional trusteeship over natural resources should require public authorities to act transparently, sustainably and accountably, with proper regard to both present and future generations. These are not foreign concepts being introduced into Ghanaian constitutional law. Their foundations are already present. Article 36(9) requires the State to take appropriate measures to protect and safeguard the national environment for posterity. And Article 41(k) imposes a corresponding duty upon citizens to protect and safeguard the environment. 7 Therefore, the Constitution already speaks both of trusteeship and posterity. The missing step is to connect the two more clearly as proposed by the CRC. The position of the Government, rather, promotes a disconnection. The Case for Constitutional Principle Government’s strongest argument is that the Committee’s objectives can largely be achieved through legislation. In many instances, that is correct. The Lands Act, 2020 (Act 1036), the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703), the Water Resources Commission Act, 1996 (Act 522), the Land Use and Spatial Planning Act, 2016 (Act 925), the Fisheries Act, 2002 (Act 625), and the Environmental Protection Act, 2025 (Act 1124) provide substantial regulatory machinery. 8 But the existence of legislation does not resolve the constitutional question. While ordinary legislation supplies the machinery for governance, a Constitution establishes the foundational principles within which that machinery must operate. Consequently, Parliament retains the power to amend or repeal statutes, whereas constitutional obligations uniquely bind the legislature itself. The distinction becomes particularly important where natural resources are concerned because decisions taken today may have consequences extending far beyond the life of a government or Parliament. A forest destroyed cannot always be recreated. A polluted water body may require generations to recover. An exhausted mineral deposit cannot be mined twice. Some decisions are effectively irreversible. The case for constitutional protection therefore rests not upon a distrust of legislation but upon the peculiar character of the subject matter. Statutory Precedents for Intergenerational Responsibility Government’s preference for legislation also sits alongside an important development in Ghanaian statutory law. The Petroleum Revenue Management Act, 2011 (Act 815) requires petroleum revenue to be managed in a responsible, transparent, accountable and sustainable manner for the benefit of the citizens of Ghana. 9 It also established the Ghana Petroleum Funds, including the Ghana Heritage Fund, thereby giving statutory expression to the principle that exhaustible resource wealth should not be consumed exclusively by the present generation. The Minerals Development Fund Act, 2016 (Act 912) reflects another aspect of the same idea. Its stated object includes providing financial resources for the direct benefit of mining communities, persons holding interests in land within those communities, and traditional and local government authorities in mining areas. 10 Its Section 3 provides that among the Fund’s sources, twenty per cent (20%) of mineral royalty received by the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) from holders of mining leases. The Land Use and Spatial Planning Act, 2016 (Act 925), similarly places sustainable development and the judicious use of land within Ghana’s planning framework. 11 These enactments reveal something important that intergenerational responsibility, sustainability and community benefit are not novel constitutional theories imported from elsewhere. They already inform Ghanaian legislation. The CRC’s proposal was, in that respect, an invitation to gather existing national commitments into a coherent constitutional principle. Reconceptualising Environmental Protection within the Directive Principles Article 36(9) represents an important constitutional commitment to environmental protection. Its location within the Directive Principles of State Policy, however, raises the familiar question of enforceability. The Supreme Court has considered the constitutional status of the Directive Principles in cases including New Patriotic Party v. Attorney-General , the CIBA case, and Ghana Lotto Operators Association v. National Lottery Authority . 12 The law demonstrates that the Directive Principles form part of the constitutional architecture and cannot simply be dismissed as political aspirations. Yet, there remains a difference between a directive to the State and an express constitutional right vested in a person. That difference matters to a community whose source of drinking water have been polluted, a farmer whose land has become unproductive because of extractive activity, or a coastal settlement confronting severe environmental degradation. The constitutional review process should therefore consider an express right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. Such a right need not turn every breach of environmental legislation into a constitutional action. Parliament would remain responsible for environmental standards, permitting systems, environmental assessments and enforcement procedures. The constitutional right would instead provide the ultimate legal standard against which grave environmental injury and governmental failure may betested. This would complement, rather than displace, the Environmental Protection Act, 2025. Ex-Ante Resource Governance: The strategic Value of Prior Parliamentary Review The Committee also proposed strengthening Article 268 by requiring parliamentary approval before the Executive signs natural resource concessions or grants. Government rejects this recommendation, relying substantially on the Supreme Court’s interpretation of Article 268 in Ndebugre v. Attorney-General . 13 The reliance on Ndebugre does not entirely answer the question. Here, the Supreme Court was concerned with what Article 268 means and how the existing requirement of parliamentary ratification operates. The constitutional review exercise asks a different question, namely whether Article 268 should continue to operate in precisely that manner. Therefoe, a judicial interpretation of the Constitution cannot itself foreclose an amendment to the Constitution. There is also a practical consideration. Once the Executive has negotiated and executed a major resource agreement, contractual expectations arise. Investments may be planned and political pressure may develop around ratification. Parliament is then asked to review an arrangement which has already acquired considerable momentum. Prior approval for transactions of exceptional national importance would allow parliamentary scrutiny before the State becomes committed. This need not apply to every transaction. The Constitution or implementing legislation could prescribe appropriate thresholds based on value, duration, strategic importance or the nature of the resource concerned. Government could therefore accept the principle while refining the Committee’s proposal. Institutional Proliferation vs. Regulatory Coherence under Article 269 Government also rejects the proposed coordinating authority for natural resources because it fears the creation of another layer of bureaucracy. It considers that coordination can be achieved through executive direction, particularly since the heads of the relevant commissions are presidential appointees. 14 The first concern is legitimate. Ghana should not create a constitutional commission whenever existing institutions fail to coordinate effectively. But the proposed alternative is less satisfactory. Natural resources do not fall neatly within administrative boundaries. A mining operation may involve mineral rights, land tenure, water resources, forestry, environmental permitting, spatial planning, local government and community interests. Different institutions may lawfully exercise authority over different aspects of the same ecosystem. Article 269 itself recognises the need for coordination. It requires the relevant natural resource commissions to regulate and manage resource utilisation and coordinate policy relating to those resources. 15 The problem is therefore already constitutional in character. Government could meet its own objection without abandoning the Committee’s objective. Instead of creating a new Natural Resources Commission, the Constitution could impose a clear coordinating obligation while Parliament assigns the function to an existing institution or creates an inter-agency mechanism by statute. Securing Local Equity in Mineral Wealth The CRC proposed allocating a percentage of gross mineral revenue to mining communities. Government, on the other hand, considers this a matter better regulated by legislation. 16 On the question of fixing a percentage permanently in the Constitution, Government has a respectable argument – mineral prices change, fiscal conditions change and revenue arrangements require some flexibility. The principle underlying the recommendation is harder to dismiss. Parliament itself recognised that principle when it enacted the Minerals Development Fund Act, 2016 (Act 912). The Act expressly provides for resources to benefit mining communities and identifies twenty per cent of mineral royalties received by the State as a source of the Fund. 17 Mining communities often bear costs that are not distributed evenly across the country. Land may be lost to extraction, water systems affected, livelihoods disrupted and local infrastructure placed under pressure. Those communities should have a legally secured interest in the wealth extracted from their surroundings. The Constitution need not prescribe the percentage. It could instead establish the principle that communities directly affected by natural resource exploitation are entitled to an equitable share of the resulting public benefits, with Parliament determining the formula by legislation. That approach preserves fiscal flexibility while protecting distributive justice. A Pragmatic Approach to Ecocide to Integrate Criminal Accountability with Economic Governance Government also rejects constitutionalisation of the Committee’s proposal for an offence of ecocide, taking the view that environmental offences can be dealt with through existing legislation. 18 Here, Government’s caution is partly justified. The Constitution is not a criminal code. The elements of an offence, the required mental element, available defences, penalties and prosecutorial arrangements are properly matters for legislation. However, it does not follow that the constitutional objective should beabandoned. Ghana’s experience with illegal mining (Galamsey) demonstrates that environmental destruction can assume a scale beyond an ordinary regulatory infraction. The contamination of major water systems, destruction of forest reserves and extensive degradation of agricultural land can threaten communities and impose enormous restoration costs upon the State. A more measured constitutional response would require Parliament to legislate against grave, widespread or long-term environmental destruction while leaving the precise offence and punishment to statute. Government’s legitimate concern about constitutional detail would then be answered without losing the substance of the Committee’s recommendation. Expanding the Constitutional Scope of Marine Regulation The Committee’s proposal for constitutional attention to ocean governance and the blue economy was similarly rejected by the Government when it considered existing legislation, including the Fisheries Act, sufficient to address the subject. 19 That approach understates the modern significance of Ghana’s maritime domain. Ocean governance now concerns far more than fisheries. It encompasses offshore petroleum, shipping, ports, marine pollution, coastal development, biodiversity, tourism, coastal protection, climate adaptation and emerging blue-carbon interests. The Constitution itself recognises Ghana’s territorial sea, continental shelf and exclusive economic zone when vesting natural resources under Article 257(6). 20 The maritime domain is therefore already part of Ghana’s constitutional conception of its natural wealth. A constitutional provision on ocean governance need not regulate fishing seasons or marine permits. Those matters properly belong to legislation. It could instead require sustainable use of marine resources, protection of marine ecosystems, prevention of pollution and due regard to the livelihoods and resilience of coastal communities. Once again, the Constitution would state the principle. Parliament would provide the machinery. Transparency as an Incident of Trusteeship There is another matter which should feature more prominently in the reform discussion. If natural resources are held in trust for the people, the people should ordinarily be entitled to know how those resources are being disposed of and managed. Article 21(1)(f) guarantees the right to information, subject to qualifications necessary in a democratic society. The Right to Information Act, 2019 (Act 989) gives statutory effect to that constitutional guarantee. 21 Natural-resource governance presents a particularly strong case for transparency. Subject to legitimate protections for commercially sensitive information, the public should have meaningful access to resource agreements, beneficial ownership information, environmental obligations, rehabilitation commitments and the revenues accruing to the State. This follows naturally from the idea of trusteeship. A public trustee who disposes of resources belonging beneficially to the people should be accountable to those people for the terms upon which that power is exercised. Meeting Government’s Concern Through Effective Legislative Compromises That Preserve Reform Intent The Government Position Paper proceeds from an understandable concern. It does not wish to overload the Constitution with matters better handled by Parliament. That concern should inform the final reform. It should not determine it. Consequently, some of the CRC recommendations can plainly be refined. A fixed percentage of mineral revenue need not be constitutionalised. The ingredients of ecocide should remain statutory. A new Natural Resources Commission may be unnecessary. Technical environmental standards should remain within the Environmental Protection Act and subsidiary legislation. The solution lies in distinguishing constitutional principle from statutory machinery . The Constitution may establish public trusteeship while leaving land administration to the Lands Act. It may protect the entitlement of mining communities while leaving Parliament to determine the revenue formula. It may require integrated resource governance without creating another commission. It may recognise the gravity of catastrophic environmental destruction while leaving criminal definitions and penalties to legislation. It may guarantee a healthy environment while leaving technical environmental standards to Act 1124. That approach preserves constitutional economy without sacrificing constitutional purpose. The Need to Realign the Constitution with the Pressing Demands of a Changing Socio- Ecological Landscape The 1992 Constitution was adopted more than three decades ago. Its provisions on natural resources and the environment were significant for their time and remain important. Ghana, however, now confronts circumstances materially different from those of 1992. The country has become a petroleum producer. Mining has expanded in scale and complexity. Galamsey has become one of the gravest environmental governance problems of the Fourth Republic. Pressure on forests, agricultural lands and water bodies has intensified. Coastal communities face increasing environmental pressures. Parliament itself has responded by enacting substantial legislation on petroleum revenue, land administration, spatial planning, mining-community development and environmental protection. The law has moved because the country has moved. The Constitution, therefore, should not remain static merely because statutes have developed beneath it. The constitutional review exercise presents a rare opportunity to decide which principles governing Ghana’s natural resources are sufficiently important to bind governments beyond an electoral term. Government is right to resist unnecessary constitutional detail. It should nevertheless reconsider its broad rejection of the Committee’s natural-resource and environmental proposals. There is a reasonable middle ground where existing institutional design may largely remain. Thus, technical regulation may remain with Parliament. And what the Constitution should do is to strengthen a limited set of enduring principles: public trusteeship, sustainability, intergenerational equity, meaningful community participation, equitable sharing of resource benefits, transparency, integrated natural resource governance and an enforceable right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. None of these ideas is alien to Ghanaian law. Their foundations already appear, although separately, in Articles 36, 41, 257, 268 and 269 of the Constitution, the Petroleum Revenue Management Act, the Minerals Development Fund Act, the Land Use and Spatial Planning Act, the Lands Act and the Environmental Protection Act. The task is to draw those scattered commitments together into a coherent constitutional settlement. Natural resources may be exploited in the present, but the consequences of their exploitation are inherited by the future. A Constitution which expressly requires the State to protect the environment for posterity cannot be indifferent to that fact. Government still has an opportunity to reconsider its position. It should do so. REFERENCES AND AUTHORITIES [1] [2] [5] [14] [16] [18] [19] Government of Ghana, Government Position Paper on the Final Recommendations of the Constitution Review Committee (2026), section 3.10.4. [3] [4] [7] [15] [20] [21] Constitution of the Republic of Ghana, 1992 [6] Rose Rameau and Abdul Baasit Aziz Bamba, ‘Reshaping Government’s Fiduciary Role Under the 1992 Constitution of Ghana’ (2024) 128 Dickinson Law Review 413. [9] Petroleum Revenue Management Act, 2011 (Act 815) [10] [17] Minerals Development Fund Act, 2016 (Act 912), ss 2 and 3. [11] Land Use and Spatial Planning Act, 2016 (Act 925). items.title: Gestion de l’eau potable et des déchets plastiques : 600 millions d’euros mobilisés pour 13 stations à Conakry, 23 dans 16 villes et 1 600 points d’eau
items.description: Le gouvernement guinéen annonce un vaste programme d’investissement de plus de 600 millions d’euros pour améliorer l’accès à l’eau potable, parallèlement à la mise en œuvre des mesures de lutte contre les déchets plastiques. Entre la remise en état de 13 stations de traitement d’eau potable à Conakry, la mise en place de 23 stations dans 16 autres villes et la réalisation de 1 600 points d’eau, les autorités affichent leur ambition de renforcer l’approvisionnement des populations. Dans le même temps, un moratoire de six mois est accordé aux acteurs de la filière plastique pour préparer leur transition vers des solutions de substitution. Ces annonces ont été faites par Faya François Bourouno, porte-parole du gouvernement, lors d’une conférence de presse conjointe des porte-parole de la Présidence et du Gouvernement, ce lundi 19 octobre 2026. Il a notamment expliqué les objectifs du décret interdisant les sachets plastiques à usage unique, les premiers résultats constatés par les autorités et les raisons du délai accordé aux industriels et aux autres acteurs concernés. Pour le porte-parole du gouvernement, cette réglementation constitue un instrument de politique publique destiné à améliorer les conditions de vie des Guinéens et à préserver leur environnement. « Ce décret, avec tout l’arsenal réglementaire qui va avec, notamment les arrêtés qui ont été pris, n’est pas un simple acte réglementaire. C’est une véritable politique publique dont l’objectif est d’améliorer le cadre et les conditions de vie de la population guinéenne », a-t-il expliqué. Selon Faya François Bourouno, cette politique doit également favoriser une évolution des modes de production et de consommation en encourageant l’utilisation de produits plus respectueux de l’environnement, notamment les emballages biodégradables. Le gouvernement affirme que les premières mesures d’application du décret ont déjà contribué à réduire la présence des déchets plastiques dans les espaces publics. Le porte-parole a présenté cette évolution comme un résultat encourageant dans la lutte contre la pollution et l’insalubrité. « Et l’application de ce décret, aujourd’hui, c’est avec beaucoup de satisfaction que nous avons l’honneur de partager avec vous le constat que nous effectuons aujourd’hui, les premiers résultats. Il y a aujourd’hui une baisse drastique constatée par nous tous des déchets plastiques dans les espaces publics. C’est une réalité, et c’est un produit de ce décret et de ses arrêtés d’application », a-t-il déclaré. Tout en mettant en avant ces premiers résultats, il a souligné la nécessité de poursuivre les efforts pour améliorer durablement la salubrité dans les villes guinéennes. Cette orientation s’inscrit, selon lui, dans la volonté du président de la République de privilégier des actions concrètes. « Pour le président de la République, chef de l’État, l’heure n’est plus à l’hésitation, l’heure est à l’action », a-t-il affirmé, précisant qu’un programme est en cours d’exécution pour accompagner l’application des mesures réglementaires. Malgré la volonté affichée de maintenir l’interdiction des sachets plastiques à usage unique, le gouvernement a décidé d’accorder un moratoire de six mois aux acteurs concernés. Ce délai doit permettre aux industriels, aux importateurs, aux commerçants et aux autres intervenants de la chaîne de valeur de préparer la transition vers des produits de substitution. Cette décision fait suite aux préoccupations exprimées par les acteurs concernés lors des échanges avec les autorités, dans le cadre d’un mécanisme de dialogue coordonné par le Premier ministre. « Et donc, la décision a été prise plutôt d’accorder un moratoire de 6 mois pour permettre au gouvernement et à tous les acteurs, les acteurs industriels, les acteurs qui interviennent dans la chaîne de valeur, de mettre en place un plan d’action et de le réaliser afin que, dans un délai de 6 mois, nous puissions réussir la transition en passant des modes de production actuels, où nous constatons la production d’emballages plastiques et d’autres déchets plastiques à usage unique, à la production de produits de substitution », a précisé Faya François Bourouno. L’objectif est de donner aux différents acteurs le temps nécessaire pour adapter leurs activités et développer des emballages ainsi que des objets capables de se dégrader de manière écologique. Le porte-parole a tenu à préciser que ce délai ne remet pas en cause les objectifs fixés par le décret. « Donc, il faut voir que ce moratoire n’est pas un abandon des mesures du décret, mais plutôt une permission temporaire permettant à tous les acteurs de converger vers cet objectif, conforme à la vision du chef de l’État », a-t-il insisté. Au-delà de la réduction de la pollution, le gouvernement entend faire de la gestion des déchets une source d’activités économiques et d’emplois. Les autorités souhaitent notamment développer les métiers liés au ramassage, à la collecte, au transport et à la valorisation des déchets. « Les déchets sont une menace, mais en voulant régler le problème des déchets, nous voulons créer des opportunités pour créer des emplois, notamment des emplois verts », a déclaré le porte-parole. Selon lui, un travail est en cours sous la coordination du Premier ministre pour structurer les différentes chaînes de valeur liées à la gestion des déchets. Cette démarche vise à créer des opportunités professionnelles, à préserver les activités industrielles et à améliorer la salubrité, particulièrement à Conakry. Faya François Bourouno a également salué la mobilisation des industriels impliqués dans la production, l’importation et la commercialisation des emballages, affirmant qu’ils travaillent avec le gouvernement pour préparer cette transition. Il a, par ailleurs, mis en avant l’adhésion de la population aux mesures engagées et annoncé la poursuite des campagnes de sensibilisation afin de favoriser des changements durables de comportement. La gestion des déchets plastiques a également été abordée sous l’angle de la préservation des ressources et de l’amélioration des conditions de vie. À ce titre, le porte-parole du gouvernement a annoncé un programme d’investissement de plus de 600 millions d’euros destiné à renforcer les infrastructures d’approvisionnement en eau potable en Guinée. « Nous avons aujourd’hui l’un des plus grands projets d’eau potable initiés dans la sous-région, avec un financement de plus de 600 millions d’euros. Et nous avons aujourd’hui tous les partenaires qui sont mobilisés autour de la Guinée pour accompagner notre pays à réussir cette transition qui va permettre à chaque citoyen guinéen d’accéder à l’eau potable », a-t-il indiqué. Ce programme comprend plusieurs volets. À Conakry, 13 stations de traitement d’eau potable doivent être remises en état. Seize autres villes du pays bénéficieront de 23 stations de traitement. À ces infrastructures s’ajoutent 1 600 points d’eau annoncés au profit des populations. Le porte-parole a rappelé que le projet avait été lancé en juin dernier par le ministère en charge du secteur. « Le mois de juin dernier, le ministère en charge de ce secteur avait lancé ce projet qui va permettre déjà, à Conakry, de remettre en état 13 stations de traitement d’eau potable, et 16 de nos villes bénéficieront aussi de 23 stations de traitement. En plus de cela, aujourd’hui, il y a 1 600 points d’eau qui sont en train d’être initiés pour le bénéfice de notre population », a-t-il expliqué. Ces investissements doivent contribuer à renforcer les capacités de production et de distribution d’eau potable, tout en améliorant l’accès des populations à ce service essentiel. Le gouvernement présente ce programme comme un levier important pour accompagner le développement du pays et améliorer les conditions de vie des citoyens. À travers le moratoire de six mois sur les plastiques et le programme d’investissement consacré à l’eau potable, le gouvernement entend agir sur deux enjeux majeurs : la réduction de la pollution et l’amélioration de l’accès aux services essentiels. Pour les autorités, l’enjeu est de concilier les impératifs environnementaux avec la préservation des activités économiques, la création d’emplois verts et l’accès des populations à l’eau potable.
